body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Unadmitted Law Graduate’s Signature Block and Law Firm Website Listing
text: A firm may list not-yet-admitted law graduates on its website and let them sign proper letters, if it clearly says they are not admitted to practice.
whatToDo: Label unadmitted graduates on your website and emails clearly, for example "Law Clerk" or "Not yet admitted to practice."
quote: A law firm may list on its website law school graduates who are not yet admitted to practice law
note: Applies Rule 7.1(a) as amended effective 2026-06-01.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Virtual law office; advertising a VLO as the lawyer’s office address
text: A New York lawyer may list a virtual office as the address in ads and online if mail reaches the lawyer there and clients can meet there on notice.
whatToDo: If you list a virtual office address, make sure you get mail sent there and can meet clients there on reasonable notice.
quote: may designate and hold out a virtual law office (“VLO”) as the lawyer’s physical office address, even if the lawyer works primarily from home in
note: Interprets Rule 7.1 as amended effective 2026-06-01; says the parts of N.Y. State 964 and 1025 (and N.Y. City 2019-2) on "principal law office" are no longer relevant.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Description of foreign lawyer who has passed bar examination but is not admitted
text: A candidate who passed the New York bar exams but is not yet admitted may describe himself as having passed the bar, with the words "passed not admitted."
whatToDo: If you are not yet admitted, say so plainly next to any statement that you passed the bar exam.
quote: may identify himself with the notation, “Passed the NY state bar examination (passed not admitted).”

body: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel (Supreme Court of Missouri)
title: use of identification as “retired (inactive) lawyer” socially
text: A retired lawyer on inactive status may use a social calling card that says "Retired (Inactive) Attorney" because it is not false or misleading.
whatToDo: If a retired lawyer lists a law title on cards, label it clearly as retired or inactive.
quote: it is the informal advisory opinion of this office that this is not false or misleading under Rule
note: Published informal opinion summary; advisory and not binding per the site. Edge of scope: a Rule 4-7.1 communication question, not marketing for clients.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Use of a Separately Registered Trade Name or DBA by a Law Firm
text: An Ohio firm may use a registered trade name or DBA in marketing without the entity designation each time, if its full legal name appears in the same medium.
whatToDo: When you market under a DBA, put the firm's full legal entity name somewhere in the same ad, website or letterhead.
quote: provided that the full legal entity name, including the entity designation, is disclosed within the same medium in which the trade name appears

body: State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct (COPRAC)
title: Practical Guidance for the Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Practice of Law
text: The guidance lists autonomous client intake as an example of agentic AI and says lawyers must not let agentic systems make legal decisions or give legal advice without lawyer review.
whatToDo: If you use an AI agent for intake, keep a lawyer reviewing its work and do not let it give legal advice to prospects.
quote: Lawyers must not deploy agentic systems in a manner that allows the system to make substantive legal determinations, communicate legal advice
note: Not a numbered formal opinion. Marketing/intake discussion is brief (one example of agentic intake); no discussion of advertising rules 7.1-7.3.

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association, Committee on Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility
title: Use of the Designation "Of Counsel"
text: A firm may list a lawyer as 'of counsel' only if there is a real, close and continuing relationship, and letterhead and marketing must describe that relationship accurately.
whatToDo: Use 'of counsel' on your website and letterhead only for lawyers with a genuine ongoing tie to the firm, and drop titles like 'Judge' for retired judges.
quote: All communications, including letterhead and marketing materials, must accurately describe the relationship and must not be false or misleading under Rule 7.1.
note: Month only, from the PBA database listing (April 2026).

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Conflicts of interest; advertising; trust account; opening a solo law practice
text: A lawyer working at a New York firm while running a New Jersey firm must follow New York ad and solicitation rules for ads aimed at New York.
whatToDo: If you advertise into New York, follow New York ad rules, show your practice limits, and avoid implying ties to another firm you work for.
quote: To the extent the inquirer intends to advertise the New Jersey law firm in New York, the New York Rules will apply to the inquirer’s
note: Advertising is one of several topics in the opinion (also conflicts and trust accounts).

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [Trade name for a digital law firm: "Contract House LLP"]
text: A trade name like 'Contract House LLP' that describes the practice area and firm form is allowed, because it is not comparative, does not suggest results and is not misleading.
whatToDo: Pick a firm or brand name that describes what you do; avoid names like 'Best Tax Lawyers' or 'Tax Fixers' that compare or promise results.
quote: It also describes the firm's practice area—contract law—as well as its organizational structure—limited liability partnership.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Solicitation; Advertisement; Lead Generators
text: Paying a platform to contact users who agreed to share their details is a permitted lead payment if it recommends no lawyer, uses neutral disclosed criteria, and fees ignore retention.
whatToDo: Before paying a lead platform, confirm it does not recommend you, picks lawyers by neutral disclosed criteria, and charges the same whether or not you are hired.
quote: The lawyer’s payment for the opportunity to make the contact is not a prohibited payment to obtain employment, but rather a permissible payment to a
note: Page heading reads "Solicitation; Advertisement; Lead Generators" but the Topic line on the page reads "Conflict analysis for per diem attorney" (apparent posting error on the NYSBA page). Builds on N.Y. State 1131 (2017).

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Chatbots and AI Agent Communications
text: Oregon lawyers may use chatbots for marketing and intake if the tool does not mislead or give legal advice, protects prospects' information, and is supervised.
whatToDo: Program your website chatbot so it never overstates your experience or results or gives legal advice, review its chats, and log prospects in your conflict system.
quote: Lawyers must be careful that chatbots do not mislead clients or prospective clients about their expertise, experience, or past results.

body: Alabama State Bar, Office of General Counsel
title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE USE: Best Practices Under Existing Professional Conduct Rules
text: The bar warns that a website chatbot giving specific legal advice without saying it is not a lawyer, and without lawyer review, may be unauthorized practice of law.
whatToDo: If your website uses a chatbot, make it say it is not a lawyer, keep it to general information, and have a lawyer review what it tells people.
quote: If the chatbot provides specific legal advice without flagging that it is not an attorney and without attorney review of its responses, this may constitute
note: General AI guidance; included only for its website-chatbot/intake example (section X, UPL). Listed by the bar among its Formal Opinions but written as best-practices guidance.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics (ACPE) Opinion 735 Supplement - Lawyer's Use of Internet Search Engine Keyword Advertising
text: After the 2025 Supreme Court ruling, lawyers may buy competitors' names as keywords, but landing pages must show a set disclaimer saying the visitor came through a paid ad.
whatToDo: If you bid on other lawyers' names, put the Court's exact paid-ad disclaimer prominently on every landing page those ads point to.
quote: The disclaimer must be prominently displayed on the landing page or pages of the lawyer or law firm website where the sponsored search result is

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Committee on Attorney Advertising
title: Testimonials (Superseding Opinion 15 and 33)
text: Testimonials are allowed if the client is identified, actors are labeled as a dramatization, results carry a 'Results may vary' line, and nothing is paid or called 'best'.
whatToDo: Name each reviewer, add the required 'Results may vary depending on your particular facts and legal circumstances' line near any results claim, and strip out words like 'best' or 'top'.
quote: where a law firm uses an actor to portray an actual and identifiable endorsing client disclosure that the depiction is a dramatization is required

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Requesting former clients to write Google reviews
text: A lawyer may ask a former client for a Google review and give a small gift, but may not write the review or tie the gift to its content.
whatToDo: Ask happy past clients for reviews, offer at most a small gift for any review, and never write it for them or reward only good ones.
quote: A lawyer may ask a former client to write a Google review of the lawyer’s services, and may offer the former client a nominal gift

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Referral fees after the 2020 rule amendments]
rules: Rule 1.4; Rule 1.6; Rule 5.4(c); Rule 8.4; former Rule 7.2(f); Utah Code Ann. 76-17-201; Utah Code Ann. 76-17-202
text: Utah lawyers may pay referral fees to lawyers and non-lawyers, including clients, if other rules are met, but must watch Utah's criminal anti-kickback law for injury claims.
whatToDo: Before paying anyone for a referral in Utah, check the current rules (a referral-fee ban was proposed in 2025) and the kickback statute, and tell clients about the arrangement.
quote: Lawyers may pay referral fees to both lawyers and non-lawyers, including clients or former clients, provided that such arrangements comply with the general requirements
note: Also answers whether Op. 22-02 should be modified for the kickback statute.

body: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel (Supreme Court of Missouri)
title: Lawyers may only use client lead generation services if the services are “qualified services” registered with the Office of Chief Disciplinary Counsel
text: A lawyer may pay an online lead company only if it is a qualified lawyer referral service registered with OCDC under Rule 4-9.1, whatever it calls its fee.
whatToDo: Before paying any lead generator in Missouri, confirm with OCDC that it is a registered qualified service under Rule 4-9.1.
quote: Any lawyer referral service used by a lawyer must be a “qualified service” in that it must conform to the requirements of Rule
note: Published informal opinion summary; advisory and not binding per the site. Cites a 2024 Missouri Supreme Court discipline decision, 701 S.W.3d 623 (lawyer names are left out of this dataset). Page renders rule numbers as '4 dash –9.1'; quote taken from a span that checkquote matched.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey
number: In re Opinion No. 735 of the Supreme Court Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics, A-61/62-19, 260 N.J. 482 (2025)
title: In re Opinion No. 735 of the Supreme Court Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics
text: Buying a competitor lawyer's name as a keyword is not by itself unethical, but the landing page reached from the ad must carry a clear disclaimer.
whatToDo: Keep competitor-name keyword campaigns only if every landing page carries the required paid-ad disclaimer.
quote: the Court requires that attorneys employing this strategy include a clear and conspicuous disclaimer on the landing page of their website when a user clicks
note: Quote is from the clerk's syllabus at the top of the official opinion PDF; the holding matches the Court's opinion as described in the ACPE 735 Supplement.

body: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel (Supreme Court of Missouri)
title: SSM messages, or similar text messages, prohibited for solicitation pursuant to Rule 4-7.3
text: Sending SMS or similar text messages to solicit people known to need legal help counts as real-time electronic solicitation and is not allowed in Missouri.
whatToDo: Do not text prospective clients you do not already know to solicit their cases; use regular U.S. mail solicitations that comply with Rule 4-7.3.
quote: SSM messaging, or similar text messaging, is not permitted by the Missouri Rule of Professional Conduct
note: Published informal opinion summary; advisory and not binding per the site.

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [Including non-lawyer business partner ads in a law firm's marketing publication]
text: A firm may run nonlawyer partners' ads in its own marketing publication if they are clearly set apart and imply no overlap or promised results.
whatToDo: Keep partner ads visibly separate from your firm's content and review each new partner ad before publishing.
quote: the Panel concludes that the inclusion of business partner organization advertisements in the Publication does not run afoul of the Rules of Professional Conduct

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Prohibited referral fees
text: Promising a non-lawyer paid "administrative" work for each case they refer is still paying for referrals, which the rules forbid.
whatToDo: Do not reward people who send you cases with paid side work or anything else of value.
quote: constitutes a thing of “value” as compensation for or as a reward for a referral and thus violates Rule 7.2(a)

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey
number: In re Opinion No. 745 of the Supreme Court Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics, A-44/45/46/47/48/49/50/51/52-23
title: In re Opinion No. 745 of the Supreme Court Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics
text: Certified New Jersey attorneys may pay referral fees to lawyers in other states even if they are not licensed in New Jersey; the Court vacated ACPE Opinion 745.
whatToDo: If you are a certified attorney, you may pay a referral fee to an out-of-state lawyer, out of and not above your reasonable fee.
quote: The Court Rules allow certified attorneys to pay referral fees to lawyers in other states even if they are not licensed here
note: Quote is from the clerk's syllabus at the top of the official opinion PDF.

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Paying a nonlawyer support-services vendor a percentage of firm revenue]
text: A Texas lawyer may not pay a nonlawyer-owned services company a percentage of firm revenue, because that shares legal fees.
whatToDo: Pay vendors flat or usage-based fees, never a percentage of your firm's revenue.
quote: A lawyer may not agree to pay a nonlawyer-owned vendor based on a percentage of the revenues of the lawyer or the lawyer's firm
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection. Vendor in the facts provides case-management and back-office services, not marketing; included because it governs percentage-based vendor pricing.

body: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions
title: Participation in 3rd-party for-profit client referral service that offers a money-back guarantee, fails to disclose the use of non-attorney actors in its advertising, and requires the lawyer to communicate with the client on the service’s online platform
text: A lawyer may not take clients from a for-profit referral service that splits a fixed fee, offers money-back guarantees, hides actors in ads, or controls lawyer-client messages.
whatToDo: Do not join referral platforms that share client fees, promise refunds if you lose, use undisclosed actors, or host your client communications.
quote: The client referral service must disclose in its advertising material whether non-attorney actors are being used

body: Washington State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Tools in Law Practice
text: Lawyers may use AI tools with competence, confidentiality and supervision; firms using intake chatbots should consider disclaimers that no lawyer-client relationship exists yet and explain whether prospects' information is confidential.
whatToDo: If a chatbot gathers intake details, add a clear disclaimer about the attorney-client relationship and confidentiality.
quote: lawyers using “chat bots” to assist with client intake by gathering preliminary information, should consider the use of appropriate disclaimers of an attorney-client relationship

body: Washington State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Use of Non-Practicing Lawyer's Name in Firm Name by Purchaser of a Law Practice
text: A lawyer who buys an entire practice may not keep the seller's name in the firm name if the seller is not associated with the buyer's firm.
whatToDo: When you buy a practice, drop the seller's name from your firm name unless the seller stays associated with your firm.
quote: may not include the name of the selling lawyer in the firm name if the selling lawyer is not associated with the purchasing lawyer’s firm

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Use of Client Information for Lawyer's Benefit
text: A lawyer pitching a client or giving a talk may describe work for a current client only with informed consent, even if the case was publicly reported.
whatToDo: Get the client's informed consent before naming them or describing their matter in a pitch or other marketing.
quote: in any form of personal marketing (or otherwise) should get informed consent from the client.

body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Lawyer-hosted parties and social events; advertising and solicitation]
text: A lawyer may host parties and social events for marketing but must follow the advertising and solicitation rules, including not giving value for recommendations.
whatToDo: Use events for marketing, but do not trade hospitality for referrals or invite people targeted from lists like arrest records.
quote: A lawyer may host parties or other social events, but when doing so must comply with rules governing lawyer advertising and solicitation.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Sharing of Legal Fees with Non-Lawyer; Impermissible Referral Fees; Non-Refundable Retainer
text: A lawyer may not use a non-lawyer bidding site that takes a percentage of the fee and claims to vet lawyers; that shares fees and pays for a recommendation.
whatToDo: Avoid client-matching sites that take a cut of your fee or claim to vet or rate the lawyers they send.
quote: if she pays a percentage of a legal fee to an online service owned by non-lawyers, on which attorneys can bid on potential clients’ legal

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Paid educational presentations marketed by a private company; later contact by viewers]
text: A lawyer may be paid for general legal education videos a company sells; the talk is not solicitation, so the lawyer may represent viewers who later call.
whatToDo: Give educational talks with a not-legal-advice warning, and let viewers contact you rather than pitching them during the talk.
quote: A lawyer who merely provides an educational presentation on general legal topics, unaccompanied by any request for professional employment, does not thereby make a "solicitation
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection. Reconsiders and clarifies a sentence in Opinion 489 (Dec. 1992) as overbroad (answering audience questions about specific problems).

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Installation of Third Party’s Self-Service Kiosk in Lawyer’s Office and Inclusion of Lawyer in Third Party’s Advertising Efforts
text: A lawyer may host a business's kiosk in the office but may not take rent or referral fees, and may appear in its ads if they meet Rule 7.4.
whatToDo: Do not take payments or referral fees from vendors in your office, and check any vendor ad that names you for specialty claims.
quote: a lawyer may be included in the business’s advertising efforts upon compliance with Rule 7.4
note: Topic "specialist-claims" assigned because the advertising part turns on Rule 7.4 (communication of fields of practice and specialization); read in summary form for that part.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Paying for a recommendation or referral
text: A paid website that says its lawyers are vetted and highly qualified recommends them, so paying to be listed is paying for a recommendation, which is not allowed.
whatToDo: Do not pay to join a directory or matching site that tells people its lawyers are vetted or the best.
quote: the lawyers’ payment to the business providing this service constitutes an improper payment for a recommendation in violation of Rule 7.2(a)

body: West Virginia Lawyer Disciplinary Board
title: Artificial Intelligence
text: Lawyers may use AI but must follow advertising rules, and a lawyer is responsible if an AI intake chatbot gives prospective clients misleading information.
whatToDo: Supervise any AI intake chatbot closely, and make sure it gives no misleading information to prospective clients.
note: General AI opinion included because its text (page 3 and footnote 3) tells lawyers to comply with advertising regulations and warns about chatbots used for intake. The official copy on the ODC website is an image-only scan with no text layer, so checkquote.py cannot verify any quote; quote is null. Text was read visually from the page images of the official PDF.

body: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions
title: Use of the terms “senior counsel,” “special counsel,” and “counsel” to describe lawyers with whom a firm has a close, regular, and personal relationship
text: A firm may call lawyers "senior counsel," "special counsel" or "counsel" if they have a close, regular, personal relationship with the firm.
whatToDo: Use counsel titles only for lawyers with a real ongoing tie to the firm, and treat shared counsel as linking the firms for conflicts.
quote: A law firm may use the terms “senior counsel,” “special counsel,” or “counsel,” as well as “of counsel,” to designate lawyers

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Referral Fees
text: Certified trial attorneys generally could not pay referral fees to out-of-state lawyers or to lawyers conflicted out of a case.
whatToDo: Do not rely on this opinion; the Supreme Court vacated it in 2025.
quote: Certified lawyers also may not pay referral fees to New Jersey lawyers who cannot accept a case, or must withdraw from a case, due to
note: Lawyer-to-lawyer referral fees, not marketing vendors.

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [Lawyer organizing and moderating a community panel]
text: A lawyer may organize and moderate a civic panel attended by possible clients because the lawyer is not acting for pay and will not market the firm or solicit attendees.
whatToDo: At community events you host, do not pitch your firm or solicit attendees in person.
quote: direct contact between attorneys and potential clients otherwise prohibited under Rule 7.3(a) may be permissible in the absence of affirmatively solicitous conduct

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey (on recommendation of the Committee on Artificial Intelligence and the Courts)
title: Legal Practice: Preliminary Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence by New Jersey Lawyers
text: The Court's preliminary AI guidelines say the existing ethics rules still apply and flag that AI will affect advertising (RPC 7.2), but leave specific advertising guidance for later.
whatToDo: Treat AI-made marketing content like any other ad under the existing rules; no NJ AI-specific ad rule exists yet.
quote: For instance, the use of AI likely will affect lawyer billing practices and advertising. See, e.g., RPC 1.5 (Fees); RPC 7.2 (Advertising).
note: Only a passing mention of advertising; included because the text names advertising.

body: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel (Supreme Court of Missouri)
title: Law firm name and retirement of lawyer
text: A firm may not keep using the name of a retired lawyer who is no longer with the firm unless the name has become a well-known trade name.
whatToDo: Remove a departed, retired lawyer's name from your firm name unless it is a recognized trade name, and keep the name truthful.
quote: may not be used to identify that law firm unless the name has become so well known that it is considered to be a trade
note: Published informal opinion summary; advisory and not binding per the site.

body: The Florida Bar, Board of Governors (Review Committee on Professional Ethics)
title: Lawyers’ use of generative artificial intelligence
text: Lawyers may use generative AI, but a chatbot that talks to prospective clients must follow the advertising rules and say it is an AI program.
whatToDo: Label any website or intake chatbot as AI, keep it from making misleading claims, and do not call your AI superior unless you can prove it.
quote: careful when using generative AI chatbot for advertising and intake purposes as the lawyer will be ultimately responsible
note: General AI opinion included because it has a "Lawyer Advertising" section on chatbots used for advertising and intake. Issuing body taken from the Bar listing context; the PDF header reads "Florida Bar Ethics Opinion".

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Use of a Lawyer’s Trade Name for Keyword Advertisements in an Internet Search Engine
text: A lawyer may not bid on another firm's unique trade name as a keyword, but may bid on a generic phrase like 'Durham family lawyers'.
whatToDo: Do not bid on competitors’ names or unique firm names; generic location-and-practice phrases are fine.
quote: the intentional selection of another lawyer’s unique firm trade name in a keyword advertisement campaign is prohibited
note: Extends 2010 FEO 14 to unique firm trade names.

body: State Bar of New Mexico, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: Practicing Law “Virtually”
text: A New Mexico lawyer may practice remotely from another state, but must not advertise an office where not licensed, and websites should state where the lawyer is licensed.
whatToDo: If you work remotely from another state, put your licensing limits on your website and letterhead and use a New Mexico mailing address.
quote: all representations, such as a website or letterhead, should clearly indicate the lawyer's jurisdictional limits

body: Maryland State Bar Association, Committee on Ethics
title: Incentive Agreements with Independent Contractors for Law Firm Advertising
text: A lawyer may not pay an outside marketing contractor a percentage of the firm's overall net income or revenue, because that is fee-splitting with a nonlawyer.
whatToDo: Pay marketing contractors a set fee, not a share of your firm's revenue or profits, and review their ads before they run.
quote: Entering into an incentive agreement with an independent contractor based on a law firm's overall financial performance constitutes fee-splitting with a non-lawyer

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Recognition of lawyer on not-for-profit organization’s website
text: A lawyer may advertise with or sponsor a nonprofit website, but may not pay to be listed on its legal-options page, because that pays for a recommendation.
whatToDo: Sponsor or advertise with nonprofits if you like, but do not pay to be listed as a suggested lawyer on their legal-help pages.
quote: A lawyer may pay for an advertisement on the website of a not-for-profit organization that provides online medical information for victims of toxic chemicals.

body: The Florida Bar, Standing Committee on Advertising
title: Guidelines for Determining Whether an Advertised Location is a Bona Fide Office
text: An ad may list only a real office the firm uses regularly; shared or hourly space may be described only as 'available by appointment' or 'for consultation'.
whatToDo: List only staffed, regularly used offices in ads; label virtual or shared spaces 'by appointment only'.
quote: The SCA has developed the following criteria for determining whether an advertised location is a bona fide office
note: Formal SCA guideline posted on the Bar's Advertising Regulation page; lists five criteria (sign, staff answering phones, full-time staff, legal services furnished there, a lawyer present regularly).

body: The Florida Bar, Standing Committee on Advertising
title: Guidelines for a Lawyer Statement of Qualifications and Experience
text: Every direct written solicitation must come with a factual statement of the lawyer's experience, including cases tried where relevant, and it must be in the same language as the ad.
whatToDo: Attach a clear statement of your experience, bar admission date and trial count to every direct mail or email solicitation, translated if the ad is not in English.
quote: If the advertisement appears in a language other than English, the statement of qualifications must appear in that language.
note: Companion SCA guidelines for a law firm's statement and for a qualifying provider's statement are on the same Bar page set and were not recorded separately.

body: The Florida Bar, Standing Committee on Advertising
title: Advertising Guidelines for Networking Sites
text: Social media used to promote a practice must follow the ad rules; paid or boosted posts must be filed, and targeted posts must meet the solicitation rules.
whatToDo: Treat business social pages as ads, file paid or boosted posts with the Bar, and follow the direct-solicitation rules for targeted posts and invitations.
quote: Pages appearing on networking sites that are used to promote the lawyer or law firm’s practice are subject to the lawyer advertising rules.
note: Committee guidelines published on the Bar advertising page; they also describe a January 31, 2020 Board of Governors decision treating targeted social media posts as targeted electronic solicitations.

body: The Florida Bar, Standing Committee on Advertising
title: Guidelines for Video Sharing Sites
text: Practice videos on sites like YouTube must follow the ad rules but need not be filed; banner ads there must be filed unless limited to safe-harbor content.
whatToDo: Keep marketing videos accurate and within the ad rules, and file any paid banner ads on video sites with the Bar.
quote: Videos appearing on video sharing sites that are used to promote the lawyer or law firm’s practice are subject to the lawyer advertising rules.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Discharged Lawyer’s Solicitation of Former Client
text: With rare exceptions, a fired lawyer may not solicit the former client to come back after the client hired a new lawyer.
whatToDo: After a client fires you and hires new counsel, do not contact the client to win the case back.
quote: a discharged lawyer may not solicit a former client to continue a client

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Departing Lawyer Reimbursing Firm for Advertising Costs
text: A firm may not make a departing lawyer pay 25% of fees on transferred cases to repay the firm's advertising costs.
whatToDo: Do not put clauses in lawyer contracts that charge departing lawyers a share of fees to recoup ad spend.
quote: The addition of 25 percent of the overall recovery of attorney fees is an impermissible restriction on the departing lawyer’s right to practice
note: Edge of scope: about recouping advertising costs, decided under Rules 1.5 and 5.6.

body: State Bar of Wisconsin, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Responding to Online Criticism
text: A lawyer may not reveal client information when answering online criticism without the client's informed consent, and usually the best move is not to respond.
whatToDo: Do not answer negative reviews with any client details; if you reply at all, keep it short, calm and free of confidential information.
quote: A response to online criticism which reveals protected information is not permitted by the self-defense exception

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Affiliation with a lawyer not admitted in New York
text: A New York lawyer may work and share fees with an out-of-state immigration lawyer in New York only if there is no unauthorized practice and nothing misleads the public.
whatToDo: When working with a lawyer not admitted in New York, make your letterhead and ads clearly show who is admitted where.
quote: the lawyers’ communications with clients and the public are not misleading
note: Advertising aspect is the requirement that public communications not mislead about admission status.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey (on recommendation of the Committee on Attorney Advertising)
title: Legal Assistance Organizations and Retention of Posted Website Materials
text: The rule that lawyers back up website content monthly and keep it three years does not bind approved legal assistance organizations, though they should keep backups.
whatToDo: Private firms: keep monthly backups of your website for three years under RPC 7.2(b).
quote: does not apply to legal assistance organizations that are approved pursuant to Rule 1 :21-11 (b ). However, legal assistance organizations should make reasonable efforts

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Solicitation of Clients by Nonprofit Legal Aid Lawyers
text: A nonprofit legal aid lawyer who gets no fee may solicit in person, and may send direct mail to people facing suit after confirming they were served.
whatToDo: If you are a no-fee legal aid lawyer, you may reach out directly, but check service of process before mailing.
quote: A nonprofit legal aid lawyer may engage in direct in-person solicitation of an individual who may benefit from representation
note: Withdraws Adv. Ops. 1990-11 and 1988-3.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: YouTube channel; general legal information; advertising
text: Making YouTube videos to educate the public is generally allowed and is not automatically advertising, but some videos could count as advertising.
whatToDo: If your videos promote your firm to get hired, treat them as ads and follow the ad rules.
quote: creating videos for a YouTube channel to educate the public or legal profession about matters of general or specific interest is a permitted activity

body: Maryland State Bar Association, Committee on Ethics
title: Internet Advertising: Competitive Keyword Purchases
text: A majority of the committee found that buying another lawyer's or firm's name as a search keyword violates Maryland's misconduct rule (Rule 8.4).
whatToDo: Do not bid on competitor lawyers' or firms' names in Maryland search-ad campaigns; remove them from keyword lists.
quote: It is the majority opinion of this Committee that the purchase of a competitor's name as a keyword in an internet marketing campaign violates
note: Majority opinion. Note the contrary New Jersey result (In re Opinion No. 735, 2025).

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Radio Data System (RDS) dashboard text ads; name-and-address requirement]
text: A very short radio dashboard ad showing only the firm name, the word "Call", and the firm phone number does not need a lawyer’s name and office address.
whatToDo: Bare-bones ads with only firm name and contact details are fine; add a lawyer name and office address once the ad says more.
quote: The use of RDS advertising with the format proposed including only the firm name, the word “Call” and the firm phone number complies with Rule
note: Page shows no issue date; year taken from the opinion number.

body: Supreme Court of Arizona, Attorney Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Responding to a former client's negative online review]
text: A lawyer may answer an online review in general terms, and reveal limited confidential information only to rebut a serious misconduct accusation, and only as needed.
whatToDo: Reply to bad reviews without client details; reveal anything confidential only to rebut a serious accusation, keep it minimal, and get ethics advice first.
quote: lawyers are free to respond to online comments in any manner that does not reveal any confidential information or violate any other ethical or legal
note: The committee's list links this opinion to a file named 'Revised Draft EO-19-0010_1-11-8-22 AH.pdf'; that linked file was read as the issued text. Arizona's committee notes its conclusion departs from most other opinions (including ABA Formal Op. 496).

body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Keyword advertising using competitors' names]
text: A lawyer may not run keyword ads using another lawyer's or firm's name or trade name without that lawyer's express consent.
whatToDo: Remove competitor names from your paid search keywords unless you have their written consent.
quote: An attorney may not utilize a keyword advertising campaign that involves using the name of another attorney, law firm

body: Connecticut Bar Association, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Referrals by a Retired Attorney
text: A retired or inactive lawyer may not be paid referral fees for matters referred after retirement; only practicing lawyers sharing responsibility may share fees.
whatToDo: Do not pay referral fees to retired or inactive lawyers, or to anyone who is not a practicing lawyer sharing responsibility under Rule 1.5(e).
quote: Regardless of whether the lawyer is retired, permanently retired, or on inactive status, payment of a referral fee for matters referred post-retirement would not be

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Responding to Negative Online Comments and Reviews
text: A lawyer generally may not reveal client information to answer a negative review, but may invite the poster to talk or point to other reviews.
whatToDo: Respond to bad reviews without any client details; invite the reviewer to call you or point readers to other reviews.
quote: A lawyer may respond to a negative online review by requesting that the person posting contact the lawyer to discuss any concerns.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Unauthorized Practice of Law: Lawyer as Mediator, Trade Names, Division of Fees with Nonlawyer
text: A lawyer and a psychologist may run a mediation service under a trade name like 'Family Mediation Center'; if it practices law, the name must meet the ad rules.
whatToDo: If your business uses a trade name and offers legal services, make sure the name is not misleading under the advertising rules.
quote: If the mediation service would not involve the practice of law, there would be no particular ethical limitation on the use of a trade name
note: Opinion is mostly about mediation and UPL; trade name is Question 3.

body: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions
title: Use of Deceased or Retired Partners' Names in Firm Name and Proper Characterization of "Of Counsel" Relationship
text: After restructuring as a PLLC, a firm may keep deceased or retired partners' names if there is continuing succession in the firm's identity.
whatToDo: Keep a retired or deceased partner's name only if the firm continues in succession, and use "of counsel" only for real ongoing relationships.
quote: a law firm may continue to use the names of its deceased or retired partners in its name provided that there has been a continuing

body: Orange County Bar Association, Professionalism and Ethics Committee
title: Attorney Bios
text: Without informed consent, a lawyer may not name a client or describe a matter in bios or marketing if it would embarrass or harm the client, nor misleadingly.
whatToDo: Get written client consent before naming clients, showing their logos, or describing their matters on your website bios.
quote: an attorney still would be precluded from listing the client representation if the listing is in any way misleading

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Inclusion on Allied Professional’s List of Recommended Lawyers
text: A lawyer may be on a doctor’s or other professional’s list of recommended lawyers if there is no referral swap and the professional does not improperly solicit for the lawyer.
whatToDo: Do not trade referrals with doctors or other professionals, and do not have them pitch your services to their patients.
quote: a lawyer may be included in an allied professional’s list of recommended lawyers provided that the professional does not disseminate the lawyer’s name and information

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: New York attorney with out-of-state office; attorney advertising and letterhead
text: A lawyer admitted in New York and Florida, with only a Florida office, may say on Florida letterhead that he is admitted in New York if not misleading.
whatToDo: State your bar admissions accurately on letterhead and ads, especially if your office is in another state.
quote: may state on the letterhead of his Florida office that he is “admitted to the New York Bar,”

body: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions
title: Lawyer participating in for-profit client matching service
text: A for-profit matching service may be used if matching is automated, it does not vouch for lawyers, stays out of the case, and its fees are reasonable and not case-linked.
whatToDo: Use a lead or matching service only if it auto-matches, does not endorse you, charges a flat fee unrelated to cases, and recheck it at each renewal.
quote: the matches are automated and completed without discretion on the part of the service as to what lawyer to match with a potential client

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Advertising in Utah by a firm with no Utah-licensed lawyer]
text: A personal-injury firm with no Utah-licensed lawyer misleads people if it advertises or solicits in Utah without a clear disclaimer that its lawyers are not licensed in Utah.
whatToDo: If none of your lawyers is licensed in Utah, put a clear licensing disclaimer on every billboard, mailer and flyer you use there.
quote: Such advertisements or solicitations may be permissible if an appropriate disclaimer or qualifying language is included.

body: State Bar of Nevada, Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility
title: Advertising Filing Requirements (coworking office space; SCR 42.1; NRPC 7.2A)
text: A Nevada lawyer may use a coworking space as a Nevada office; paid ads listing that address must say in-person meetings are by appointment only.
whatToDo: If you list a shared or coworking office in ads or on your site, say meetings are by appointment only, and keep filing paid ads with the bar.
quote: Business cards, letterhead, and websites are not within the scope of the filing requirements imposed by the Rule.

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Effect of 2020 rule changes (Rules 7.1-7.5, 5.4) on prior opinions]
text: After Utah deleted Rules 7.2-7.5, older 'false or misleading' opinions still apply, but old bans on paid referrals, fee-sharing and in-person solicitation should not be relied on.
whatToDo: Treat Utah's old advertising opinions with care: keep following the 'not false or misleading' ones, and do not rely on old bans on paid referrals or in-person solicitation.
quote: Opinions that relied upon communication being "false or misleading" are still applicable.
note: Lists which earlier opinions remain applicable, are modified, or are withdrawn (e.g., withdraws 99-04; modifies 14-02, 14-03, 14-04, 17-05).

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Conflict of interest and referral fees; real estate transaction referred by broker associated with lawyer’s real estate agency
text: A lawyer may not take real estate closings referred by an agent tied to the lawyer’s own real estate company when the agent and company split the commission.
whatToDo: Do not take legal work referred through a business you own if that business earns a commission on the same deal.
quote: A lawyer may not accept the referral of real estate closings from a real estate agent who is associated with a real estate company owned

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Firm Name; Trade Names; Assumed Names
text: A firm may use two different assumed names for separate practice areas if that is not misleading.
whatToDo: You may brand practice areas under different names, but make sure no name misleads the public.
quote: A law firm may operate under two different assumed names that distinguish separate practice areas of the firm

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Paid featured placement on Expertise.com]
text: A lawyer may not market through Expertise.com, because taking part in a listing whose site language implies the lawyer is an "expert" breaks the ad rules.
whatToDo: Do not claim, pay for, or add to a directory listing whose wording you could not lawfully use yourself.
quote: a lawyer may not adopt, endorse, claim, or contribute to any online listing that contains language or other material that would violate the Rules
note: Page shows no issue date; year taken from the opinion number.

body: State Bar of South Dakota, Ethics Committee
title: [Media misquote implying expertise or certification]
text: A lawyer is not responsible when a reporter wrongly says the lawyer claimed expertise or a specialty, but the lawyer's own website must be accurate.
whatToDo: Keep your website free of specialist or expert claims you cannot back up; you need not chase a reporter's misquote.
quote: Lawyer should, however, ensure that any statements on Lawyer’s website, such as the ones the reporter quoted, are accurate.
note: PDF is linked from statebarofsouthdakota.com/ethics-opinions/ and hosted on the bar's CMS file host (growthzonecms.com).

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Law firm associates and the phrase “and Associates” in law firm name
text: A solo lawyer may not use "and Associates" in her firm name or call lawyers from other firms her associates.
whatToDo: Use "and Associates" only if your own firm actually employs associates.
quote: may not include in her law firm name the phrase “and Associates” when she is referring to associates employed by another firm
note: No rules line shown in the posted digest.

body: State Bar of New Mexico, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: Fee Splitting when one lawyer provides no services
text: A New Mexico lawyer may not split a fee with a lawyer who only signed up the client and did no work, because that is a forbidden referral fee.
whatToDo: Do not pay another lawyer just for sending you a case; split fees only by work done or joint responsibility, with the client's written agreement.
quote: Any payment for referral (i.e., referral fee) that does not squarely fall within one of these exceptions is an impermissible referral fee prohibited by the

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Attorney advertising
text: A lawyer who asks a fertility clinic to list him on its website as a reproduction lawyer is advertising, not soliciting.
whatToDo: Treat listings you request on third-party websites as ads and follow the ad rules.
quote: to request to be included on the clinic’s website as a lawyer who practices in the area of assisted reproduction is engaged in attorney advertising,

body: New Hampshire Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: Inactive Lawyers and Referral Fees
text: An inactive lawyer may not take referral fees from an active New Hampshire lawyer for matters arising after going inactive; earlier work or clients may still be paid for.
whatToDo: Do not pay referral fees to inactive lawyers for new matters they send you.
quote: permitting payments of referral fees to inactive lawyers would not further the purpose of New Hampshire's somewhat unique referral fee rule
note: Page shows abstract and excerpt with a 'Read More' link; holding taken from the abstract.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Firm names; trade names
text: A firm may not put a dead lawyer’s name on its letterhead unless that lawyer is part of the firm’s line of succession.
whatToDo: Keep a deceased lawyer’s name only if your firm truly succeeds that lawyer’s practice.
quote: A law firm may not include on its letterhead the name of deceased attorney who does not stand in a continuing line of succession with

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Practicing Under a Common Trade Name Franchised Nationally to Lawyers and Law Firms
text: A lawyer or firm may not practice under a common trade name franchised nationally to lawyers.
whatToDo: Do not join a national law-firm franchise that has you practice under its shared brand name.
quote: A lawyer or law firm may not practice under a common trade name which is franchised nationally to lawyers.
note: Withdraws Adv. Op. 1997-1.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Advertising, solicitation, targeted email to prospective clients
text: An out-of-state firm’s email to a list of specific New Yorkers seeking clients for future class actions is both an ad and a solicitation under New York rules.
whatToDo: Treat targeted emails to specific people as solicitations and follow New York's current solicitation rules (amended June 1, 2026).
quote: seeking clients for future false advertising and products liability class actions, is both an advertisement and a solicitation under Rules 7.1 and 7.3

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Use of Domain Name Different from Name of Law Firm
text: A lawyer may use a website domain name that differs from the firm name, as long as neither one, alone or together, is misleading.
whatToDo: Pick any domain name you like, as long as it and your firm name do not mislead.
quote: An attorney may use a domain name that differs from the name of the law firm under which the attorney practices

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Responding to Negative Online Reviews
text: A lawyer may answer a client’s negative online review in a professional, restrained way but may not include confidential information.
whatToDo: Reply to bad reviews briefly and politely, never with client details, and never offer something in exchange for changing the review.
quote: a lawyer is not permitted to include confidential information in a response to a client’s negative online review

body: Delaware State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Practicing Delaware law remotely from a jurisdiction where the lawyer is not licensed]
text: Delaware lawyers may practice Delaware law remotely from another state, but may not advertise or list an office there; a local address in ads can create an office presence.
whatToDo: Do not put a home-office address in a state where you are not licensed on your website, letterhead, cards or ads.
quote: a lawyer who includes a local jurisdiction address on websites, letterhead, business cards, or advertising may be said to have established an office
note: Mainly a remote-practice opinion; included for its advertising/holding-out limits. DSBA index says the committee issued no opinions 2012-2020.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Committee on Attorney Advertising and Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics (joint)
title: Lawyers Shall Not Pay For Client Referrals; Purported "Leads" Offered by Marketing Companies May Be Disguised Referrals
text: Lawyers may pay per lead but not per client retained, and 'leads' sold with high retention rates or very high prices are really paid referrals, which are banned.
whatToDo: Before buying leads, check the price, the vendor's 'retention' claims and the contract; if you are really paying for signed clients, do not buy.
quote: Lawyers must consider factors that differentiate between a payment "per lead" and a payment "per client," beyond the mere labels used.
note: Opinion reaffirms CAA Opinion 43 (2011) on pay-per-lead.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Committee on the Unauthorized Practice of Law and Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics (joint)
title: Non-Legal Companies That Offer Legal Services to Customers Engage in the Unauthorized Practice of Law; Lawyers Who Provide Legal Services to the Company's Customers Violate the Rules of Professional Conduct
text: A company that sells flat-fee legal help and matches customers with lawyers practices law without a license; lawyers who take its cases break the ethics rules.
whatToDo: Do not take matters from companies that contract with the customer for legal services and then hand the case to you.
quote: lawyers who provide legal services to customers of such companies are assisting the company in the unauthorized practice of law

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Competitive Keyword Online Advertising
text: A lawyer may not buy another lawyer's or firm's name as a keyword for online ads.
whatToDo: Remove competitor lawyer and firm names from your paid search keyword lists.
quote: A lawyer or law firm may not purchase the name of another lawyer or law firm for use in competitive keyword online advertising.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Communication of a Lawyer Specialization in a Field of Law Not Designated by the Supreme Court
text: A lawyer could claim to be a specialist only in a field the Supreme Court of Ohio designated; the Board marks this not current after the 2024 Rule 7.4 amendment.
whatToDo: Check current Ohio Rule 7.4 before claiming a specialty; do not rely on this opinion.
quote: A communication by a lawyer that he or she is a specialist in a field of law not designated by the Supreme Court is misleading.
note: Status set to 'modified' because the Board labels it Not Current (rule changed), not formally withdrawn.

body: The Florida Bar, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Responding to negative online reviews posted by non-clients]
text: When a non-client posts a negative review, the lawyer may say the poster is not a client and the review is inaccurate, without revealing client information.
whatToDo: If a stranger reviews you, you may say they were never your client; do not discuss any real client matter.
quote: If accurate, the lawyer may state that the person who made the post is not a current client or former client.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Committee on Attorney Advertising
title: Supreme Court Committee on Attorney Advertising Reminder: Advertising Awards, Honors, and Accolades That Compare a Lawyer's Services to Other Lawyers' Services
text: Lawyers may advertise awards like Super Lawyers only if the issuer vetted them, with the methodology, issuer name and the Supreme Court 'not approved' disclaimer.
whatToDo: Check that each badge comes from a vetted selection (not pay, membership or votes) and put the methodology, issuer name and Supreme Court disclaimer right next to it.
quote: Factors such as the payment of money for the issuance of the award; membership in the organization that will issue the award
note: Notice to the Bar, not a numbered opinion. Restates and expands a May 2016 reminder.

body: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions
title: Paying a referral fee to an out-of-state lawyer
text: An Illinois lawyer may share a fee with an out-of-state lawyer who referred a personal injury case if the deal follows Illinois rules and the other state's rules.
whatToDo: When splitting a fee with a referring out-of-state lawyer, meet Illinois Rule 1.5(e) and the other state's fee-division rules.
quote: may enter into a fee-sharing agreement with an out-of-state lawyer who refers a personal injury case to the Illinois lawyer

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Firm names under amended Rule 7.1]
text: Under Utah's new Rule 7.1, a firm may use a trade name, even with a departed lawyer's name, as long as the name is not false or misleading.
whatToDo: You may keep a well-known firm name after a founder leaves or retires, but change it if that lawyer starts practicing elsewhere nearby or in the same field.
quote: The key concept in the amended Rule 7.1 is that communications regarding a lawyer's services must not be false or misleading.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Falsely advertising a partnership among law firms
text: Separate firms may not form a PLLC and advertise as members of one "Law Group," because the name would falsely suggest they practice together.
whatToDo: Do not market separate firms under a shared group name unless they really practice together.
quote: Separate and independent law firms may not form a PLLC and advertise themselves as members of “ABC Law Group PLLC”

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Rule 7.3 Solicitation of Clients
text: A lawyer may mail truthful flyers to building owners and call them, but may not email someone who already asked not to be contacted.
whatToDo: Stop contacting any prospect who says no, by any channel, and keep mailers truthful.
quote: No, it is not permissible for Lawyer to email Owner A.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Cross-Referrals, Office Sharing with Nonlawyer
text: A lawyer may not agree to send clients to a trust company in exchange for the company recommending the lawyer; simply sharing office space with a CPA is fine.
whatToDo: Do not trade client referrals with a non-lawyer business on a quid-pro-quo basis.
quote: The quid pro quo nature of Lawyer A’s above-described arrangement would clearly violate these provisions.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Disseminating Information through the Media or through Speeches
text: A lawyer may write columns, answer reader questions, appear on radio or TV and give talks if nothing is misleading and the lawyer does not pay for the exposure.
whatToDo: Media columns and talks are fine; keep them accurate and do not pay for placement as if it were free publicity.
quote: Is the above-described conduct consistent with rules of professional conduct on providing information on legal services?

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Acceptance of Referrals
text: A lawyer may accept referrals from friends and clients and may send a small thank-you gift, but not one that was promised or expected in return for referrals.
whatToDo: Send only token thank-you gifts after a referral, never as a promised reward.
quote: A gift is prohibited if offered or given in consideration of any promise, agreement or understanding that such a gift would be forthcoming

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Lawyer Membership in Business-Referral Clubs
text: A lawyer may not join a business networking club whose rules make giving referrals a condition of membership.
whatToDo: Do not join referral clubs that require you to give or follow up on referrals to keep your seat.
quote: Participation in the activities of the Association in accordance with its stated policies would violate both of those rules.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Law firm name after a partner leaves
text: A firm may keep a former partner’s name when the partner leaves for non-legal work or becomes "Of Counsel," unless the facts would make it misleading.
whatToDo: Before keeping a departed partner’s name, check that it will not mislead clients.
quote: A law firm may continue to use the name of a former partner in the firm name where the partner leaves the firm for non-legal
note: No rules line shown in the posted digest.

body: San Diego County Bar Association, Legal Ethics Committee
title: [Networking group vs. lawyer referral service]
text: A lawyer may not join a networking group that caps lawyer seats, bars other groups and pressures referrals, because it acts as an unlicensed referral service.
whatToDo: Skip referral clubs that require a quota of referrals or give you an exclusive seat; ordinary networking groups are fine.
quote: A lawyer may not be a member of a networking group that (1) limits the number of lawyer members

body: American Bar Association, Standing Committee on Ethics and Professional Responsibility
title: Responding to Online Criticism
text: A lawyer may not reveal client information to answer a bad online review; a review alone does not trigger self-defense, so stay silent or reply without client details.
whatToDo: Do not reply to negative reviews with any client details; either stay silent, ask the site to remove false posts, or post a short reply inviting private contact.
quote: As a best practice, lawyers should consider not responding to a negative post or review, because doing so may draw more attention to it
note: Full text of the ABA opinion read from a copy hosted by the Colorado Bar Association (linked from cobar.org Formal Ethics Opinions page next to CBA Op. 136). americanbar.org returned HTTP 403 to fetch.py, so the ABA's own copy was not read; evidence S because the host is not the ABA.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Lawyer paying for recommendation
text: A lawyer may not join an online matching service that vouches for the lawyer and recommends him as the "best lawyer" for the person.
whatToDo: Do not pay services that tell people you are the best lawyer for them.
quote: A lawyer may not participate in an internet lawyer-client matching service that vouches for the lawyer’s credentials, competence and effectiveness

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Paying an annual fee to be listed as an "identified" closing-lawyer provider on bank loan forms]
text: A lawyer may pay a flat $249 yearly fee to be listed as an identified service provider on banks’ loan forms, as a reasonable cost of advertising.
whatToDo: Flat-fee listings in provider networks are fine; avoid paying per referral or per closing.
quote: Lawyer A may pay the fee and participate in Company’s network of legal service providers and be “identified” as a possible service provider
note: Page shows no issue date; year taken from the opinion number.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Lawyer or Law Firm Use of Service Mark
text: A firm may register and advertise a service mark if not misleading, but may not use 'pro' or 'pros' in it and must pair it with the firm's legal name.
whatToDo: Use a service mark only next to your firm's formal name, and keep "pro" or "pros" out of it.
quote: A lawyer or law firm may register and use a service mark in communications and advertising.

body: New Hampshire Bar Association, Ethics Committee
number: Ethics Corner: Online Presence and Client Confidences
title: Online Presence and Client Confidences
text: Lawyers may market on social media under the ad rules, should note posts are not legal advice, and may not reveal confidences when answering negative reviews.
whatToDo: Add a 'not legal advice / no attorney-client relationship' disclaimer to posts and ads, and answer bad reviews without any client details.
quote: In your advertising and social media interactions, you would be prudent to include a disclaimer that the advertisement does not convey legal advice or create
note: Ethics Corner commentary (general guidance), not a numbered Ethics Committee opinion.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Solicitation and Referral of Real Estate Matters by Real Estate Broker Employed by Lawyer as Paralegal
text: A lawyer may take closings referred by her paralegal-broker if the lawyer has no stake in the commission, handles conflicts, and keeps the paralegal from improper solicitation.
whatToDo: Make sure staff who refer clients to you follow the solicitation rules.
quote: The lawyer must also ensure that the paralegal’s conduct complies with Rule 7.3 governing attorney solicitation

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Firm names; trade names
text: After the June 2020 rule change, a New York firm may use a trade name with no lawyer's name, and may keep a retired name partner, if not misleading.
whatToDo: You may use a trade name for your firm, as long as it is not false or misleading.
quote: A law firm may practice in New York using a name that does not include the name of any lawyer currently or formerly practicing in
note: Interprets Rule 7.5(b) as amended by the Appellate Divisions’ Joint Order of June 24, 2020.

body: Alaska Bar Association, Ethics Committee (adopted by Board of Governors)
title: What Are Counsel's Ethical Duties Regarding Publicizing Client Recoveries?
text: A personal-injury lawyer may run ads with client testimonials that state recovery amounts only if the clients give informed consent.
whatToDo: Get informed client consent before any ad or testimonial mentions a client's recovery amount.
quote: Testimonials disclosing amounts of recoveries are consistent with the Alaska Rules of Professional Conduct only if the clients provide informed consent.

body: The Florida Bar, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Responding to a negative online review by a former client]
text: A lawyer may not reveal client information when answering a negative online review, but may say the review is not fair or accurate and that the lawyer cannot respond fully.
whatToDo: Answer bad reviews only with a short, general statement and never reveal client details.
quote: may respond with a general statement that the lawyer is not permitted to respond as the lawyer would wish, but that the online review is
note: The PDF heading reads "OPINION 20-01"; the Bar index lists it as Opinion 20-1.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Trade Name Used as Law Firm Name
text: A firm may use a trade name, but not one that implies results, speed, or a link to a government, nonprofit or charity.
whatToDo: If you use a trade name, make sure it does not promise results or suggest a government or charity connection.
quote: A trade name that implies certain results, expediency, or a connection to a governmental, nonprofit, or charitable organization is inherently false or misleading

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Using a nonlawyer employee to staff an advertising booth after hail storms]
text: A staffer may run a booth with signs and brochures, but neither lawyer nor staffer may start conversations about hiring the firm, and no bonus per new client.
whatToDo: At events, let people come to you, train staff not to start the pitch, and never pay staff per signed client.
quote: The lawyer may not pay the nonlawyer staff any bonus or additional compensation for enlisting one or more clients as a result of the nonlawyer's
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Lawyer Departing Law Firm
text: A firm and a departing lawyer may notify affected clients, and the notice may say the lawyer or firm is willing to keep handling the matter.
whatToDo: When a lawyer leaves, send clients a neutral notice of the departure and respect the client's choice of counsel.
quote: The notice may indicate the availability and willingness of the lawyer or law firm to continue to provide legal services to the client
note: Withdraws Adv. Op. 98-05.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Use of Surname of Retiring or Inactive Lawyer in Law Firm Name and Letterhead
text: A firm may keep a retired or inactive lawyer's surname in its name in a line of succession, and list that lawyer on letterhead with the registration status.
whatToDo: If you keep a retired partner's name on letterhead, label the person as retired or inactive.
quote: A law firm may continue to include in the firm name, in a continuing line of succession, the surname of a retiring lawyer
note: Withdraws Adv. Op. 91-18 and modifies Adv. Op. 96-3.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Attorney website to assist pro se litigants; marketing of legal services
text: A lawyer may run a separate automated self-help filing website if it gives no individual advice and does not advertise the law firm; lawyer review brings in all lawyer rules.
whatToDo: Keep any automated self-help website separate from your firm’s marketing, or treat it as part of your law practice.
quote: establish a separate business through a website to assist pro se litigants with filings through an automated system

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Law firm name
text: Under the pre-June 2020 rule, New York-only lawyers could not use a trade name, but could truthfully advertise ties to an out-of-state firm that uses one.
whatToDo: Check the later Opinion 1207 before relying on this; trade names became allowed in New York after June 2020.
quote: may truthfully advertise its affiliation with an out-of-state firm that uses a trade name permitted in the other jurisdiction

body: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions
title: Named partner in full-time nonlegal employment and no longer practicing law.
text: A firm name may not imply a partnership that does not exist or mislead the public, and generally should not include a lawyer who no longer practices.
whatToDo: Take a non-practicing lawyer's name out of the firm name and do not imply a partnership you do not have.
quote: A law firm's name may not imply a partnership when none exists.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Committee on Attorney Advertising
title: Geo-Fencing, Geo-Targeting, and Similar Electronic Advertising Techniques
text: Geo-targeted digital ads are allowed, but not at hospitals, funeral homes, police stations, courthouses or accident sites, not aimed at disaster victims, and not as forced-view pop-ups.
whatToDo: Exclude sensitive locations from geo-fence campaigns and run only ads that sit beside page content, never ones users must sit through.
quote: These areas include, but are not limited to, emergency rooms, hospitals, urgent care centers, funeral homes, police stations, courthouses, and accident sites.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Freelance or per diem attorney; trade names; maintenance of bank accounts and records; conflicts
text: A lawyer marketing freelance per diem work to other lawyers may use the name and domain "Surname Esquire."
whatToDo: A freelance name that uses your own surname is fine; keep it truthful.
quote: may use the name and domain name Surname Esquire

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Asking clients for positive online reviews and star ratings]
text: A lawyer may ask clients to post good online reviews, but must not encourage false statements and should try to fix any that appear.
whatToDo: Ask clients for honest reviews, give nothing in return, and act to correct or remove any false review you learn about.
quote: a Texas lawyer may ask current and former clients to post favorable star ratings and online reviews about the lawyer
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection. Facts assume the lawyer gives nothing of value for reviews; the opinion does not address reviews from vendors, employees, friends or family.

body: New York County Lawyers Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Ethical Obligations when Lawyers Work Remotely
text: A New York firm may work fully remotely; a firm that keeps a physical New York office may list it as its principal law office address under Rule 7.1(h).
whatToDo: If your firm works remotely, keep a qualifying New York office address and use it as the principal office address in your ads and website.
quote: Opinion 2019-2 does not suggest that there is any ethical impropriety if a law firm that currently maintains a physical office space in New York
note: Mainly a remote-work opinion; included only for its short Rule 7.1(h) principal-office-address discussion (para. 2). The opinion's own rules line lists 1.1, 1.6, 5.1, 5.3; 7.1(h) is discussed in the text. Borderline for scope; drop if the dataset wants advertising-focused opinions only.

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Competitive keyword advertising using competitors’ names]
text: A lawyer may buy other lawyers’ and firms’ names as search keywords, but the ads must follow all ad rules and must not be derogatory or uncivil.
whatToDo: You may bid on competitor names, but keep the ad text truthful and never imply you are the competitor or knock them.
quote: A lawyer may use internet competitive keyword advertising that includes the names of competing lawyers and law firms.
note: Reaches the opposite result from North Carolina 2010 FEO 14. Page shows no issue date; year taken from the opinion number.

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Use of retired lawyers’ names in a successor firm name]
text: A new firm that is a bona fide successor to the old firm may keep the names of retired lawyers in its firm name.
whatToDo: Keep retired partners’ names in the firm name only if the new firm is a true successor of the old one.
quote: Lawyer D may use the names of retired lawyers A and B in the new firm name, formed subsequent to B’s retirement.
note: Page shows no issue date; year taken from the opinion number.

body: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel (Supreme Court of Missouri)
title: requirement to disclose Of Counsel association
text: When a lawyer is Of Counsel to two firms, both firms' ads, websites, letterhead and the lawyer's cards and online profiles must disclose both Of Counsel ties.
whatToDo: If a lawyer is Of Counsel to more than one firm, show every Of Counsel relationship on all ads, website listings, letterhead and profiles.
quote: Attorney’s business cards, online profiles, and other materials must disclose that Attorney is associated with both firms in Of Counsel relationships
note: Published informal opinion summary; advisory and not binding per the site. Only the year (2020) is shown as the adoption date.

body: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel (Supreme Court of Missouri)
title: duties upon leaving a law firm
text: When a lawyer leaves, the firm should promptly update its ads, website and firm name so they do not mislead about who is with the firm.
whatToDo: When a lawyer leaves, update your website, ads and firm name right away.
quote: Firm lawyers should promptly update advertising materials, the firm’s website, the firm’s name if necessary, and other communications
note: Published informal opinion summary; advisory and not binding per the site. Only the year (2020) is shown. Advertising point is one part of a broader departing-lawyer opinion.

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Advertising Inclusion in Self-Laudatory List or Organization
text: A lawyer may advertise being on a "best lawyers" type list or in a laudatory organization, subject to conditions set out in the opinion.
whatToDo: Advertise awards only when they meet the opinion’s conditions, such as legitimate standards and clear identification of who gave the award.
quote: a lawyer may advertise the lawyer’s inclusion in a list or membership in an organization that bestows a laudatory designation on the lawyer subject to
note: Pre-2020 by number but adopted October 2019; controlling North Carolina opinion on awards. The exact conditions were read only in summary form; read the full opinion before relying on them.

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Offering Incentive to Engage with Law Practice’s Social Networking Sites
text: A lawyer may not offer prize entries for "likes" or follows when the platform shows that activity to other users, because it pays for what looks like a recommendation.
whatToDo: Do not run giveaways that reward people for liking, following, or sharing your firm’s social media.
quote: offering an incentive to engage with a law practice’s social media account is misleading and constitutes an improper exchange for a recommendation
note: Pre-2020 landmark on social media incentives.

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [Paying a digital marketing agency per title order referred by a mortgage broker]
text: A lawyer may not pay a marketing agency $200 for each title order a mortgage broker sends, because that is really paying for the broker's ads in exchange for referrals.
whatToDo: Never pay a marketer or third party per referral you receive from someone else; pay only for your own advertising.
quote: The inquiring attorney effectively pays the mortgage broker's costs of advertising in exchange for title orders.

body: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Legal Ethics
title: Virtual Law Office and Use of Executive Office Suites
text: A lawyer may use a virtual or shared office, but any office listed in ads must be where the lawyer really works, not a front to look bigger or local.
whatToDo: List only office addresses where you actually meet clients and do legal work; do not list rented suites just to appear in more towns.
quote: A lawyer may not list alternative or rented office spaces in public communications for the purpose of misleading prospective clients
note: Opinion mostly covers confidentiality and supervision; only the office-listing part is about marketing. The 2013 committee date and 2019 court approval date are both printed on the PDF.

body: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Legal Ethics
title: Lawyer Advertising and Solicitation (compendium opinion)
text: This compendium covers actors in ads, "no recovery, no fee", third-party praise, case results, referral services, "Best Lawyers" listings, and "specialist" claims under Virginia’s misleading-ads rule.
