whatToDo: Check every ad against LEO 1750; for example, disclose when an actor plays a lawyer or client.
quote: failing to disclose that the actor is not truly an employee or member of the law firm, when the language used implies otherwise, is misleading
note: Pre-2020 by approval date but still the controlling Virginia advertising compendium; the Bar’s ethics page says obsolete Legal Advertising Opinions were withdrawn in 2018 or folded into LEO 1750. Topics specialist-claims, domain-trade-names and referral-marketing-fees are also covered in sections not quoted here.

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [Paying a for-profit internet "lawyer referral service" per lead]
text: A lawyer may not pay a for-profit online company that calls itself a 'Lawyer Referral Service' for leads, because only not-for-profit bar-approved referral services may be paid.
whatToDo: Before paying an online lead company, check that it is not acting as a for-profit referral service; Rhode Island allows paying only bar-approved nonprofit services.
quote: A lawyer who participates in an internet lawyer referral service that is not a not-for-profit lawyer referral service violates Rule 7.2(c).
note: The Panel expressly did not decide the exclusivity or flat-fee-per-lead questions.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey (on recommendation of the Committee on Attorney Advertising)
title: Amendments to Attorney Advertising Guideline 1
text: Every lawyer ad must include contact information, which may now be a website URL as well as an address, phone, fax or email.
whatToDo: Make sure every ad shows at least one contact point for the firm, such as a phone number or website URL.
quote: In any advertisement by an attorney or law firm, the advertisement shall include contact information for the attorney or law firm.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Lawyer's Use of Internet Search Engine Keyword Advertising
text: A lawyer may buy a competitor's name as a keyword, but may not hyperlink the competitor's name so it secretly sends users to the lawyer's own site.
whatToDo: Never redirect searches for another lawyer's name or URL to your site; see the 2025 court ruling for the landing-page disclaimer now required.
quote: Redirecting a user from the competitor's website to the lawyer's own website is purposeful conduct intended to deceive the searcher for the other lawyer's website.

body: New York State Bar Association, Commercial and Federal Litigation Section (Social Media and New Communication Technologies Committee)
title: Social Media Ethics Guidelines of the Commercial and Federal Litigation Section of the New York State Bar Association
text: A lawyer's business or personal social media profile may fall under the advertising and solicitation rules when it is used to talk about the lawyer's services.
whatToDo: Treat any social media profile where you mention your services as advertising and follow the ad and solicitation rules.
quote: may be subject to attorney advertising and solicitation rules. If the lawyer communicates concerning her services using her social media profile
note: Section guidelines, not an ethics-committee opinion; the PDF states they do not represent NYSBA views unless adopted by the House of Delegates or Executive Committee. Quote is from Guideline No. 2.A. Earlier editions (2014, 2015) are also linked on the Section page.

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [In-person solicitation of neighborhood business owners]
text: A lawyer may visit businesses in person to seek work, since Rule 7.3 exempts business organizations, but the handout is an ad that must be filed with disciplinary counsel.
whatToDo: You may pitch local businesses face to face; file a copy of any handout with disciplinary counsel as Rule 7.2 requires.
quote: Rule 7.3 , which prohibits in-person contact with prospective clients for solicitation of professional employment, contains an exception for business organizations.

body: New Hampshire Bar Association, Ethics Committee
number: Ethics Corner: Lawyers and Texting, Part V
title: Lawyers and Texting: Part V - Ethics of Advertising via Text Messaging
text: New Hampshire's rules do not appear to bar text-message ads or solicitations that follow the written-ad rules, name the lawyer and office, and say 'advertising' when soliciting.
whatToDo: Put your name, firm and address in every marketing text, label solicitation texts 'advertising', and avoid unwanted or costly texts.
quote: the lawyer should include a disclosure that the text message is "advertising" in any message issued as a direct solicitation of a prospective client
note: Ethics Corner commentary (general guidance), not a numbered Ethics Committee opinion.

body: Colorado Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: A Lawyer's Response to a Client's Online Public Commentary Concerning the Lawyer
rules: Colo. RPC 1.6; Colo. RPC 1.6(b)(6); Colo. RPC 1.8(b); Colo. RPC 1.9; Colo. RPC 1.18
text: A Colorado lawyer may answer a negative review, but may reveal client information only if the review creates a real controversy, and only what is reasonably needed.
whatToDo: Answer bad reviews briefly without client details; the safest reply says you cannot discuss the matter and disagree with the post.
quote: a lawyer may respond if the online criticism creates a "controversy" between the lawyer and the client
note: Pre-2020 landmark: widely cited as the minority view on online-review responses.

body: Kentucky Bar Association, Ethics Committee (adopted by the Board of Governors)
title: Proposed self-defense opinion
text: A lawyer may not reveal client information to answer a former client's online criticism; usually ignore it or post a short reply citing confidentiality.
whatToDo: Do not argue the facts with an unhappy client online; ignore the review or post a short note that you cannot discuss client matters.
quote: In most instances the best advice is to ignore the criticism
note: Issued 2019; included as Kentucky's controlling opinion on responding to negative online reviews.

body: Kentucky Bar Association, Ethics Committee (adopted by the Board of Governors)
title: Disclosure of Information on Social Media
text: Without client consent, a lawyer may not reveal a client's identity or case information in a blog or social media post, even if it is in a public record.
whatToDo: Get written client consent before naming a client or describing a case in any blog or social post.
quote: there is no justification for revealing information, without consent, about past or present clients in a blog or other social media
note: Issued 2019; included as Kentucky's controlling opinion on client information in lawyer blogs and social media.

body: State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct (COPRAC)
title: Attorney Directory and Rating Websites
text: A lawyer is not responsible for a directory profile until adopting or using it; then it must be truthful, with no fake reviews and care over misleading testimonials.
whatToDo: If you claim or link to a directory profile (Avvo-type), check it for false content, never have friends or family post reviews, and add a disclaimer near testimonials.
quote: When an attorney uses the profile to market the attorney’s practice, the profile becomes a communication about the attorney’s services

body: San Diego County Bar Association, Legal Ethics Committee
title: [Marketing program offering brief limited-scope phone consultations]
text: A lawyer may not join a for-profit program that collects a consumer's flat fee and keeps a 'marketing fee'; that is fee-sharing and an uncertified referral service.
whatToDo: Before joining any online consult platform, confirm it is a State Bar-certified referral service or that you pay only a flat advertising cost, never a cut of the legal fee.
quote: California lawyers who participate in a plan like Company’s violate Rule 5.4.

body: Nebraska Lawyers' Advisory Committee
title: [Trade name or service mark without professional entity designation]
text: A law firm may use a trade name without its LLC or LLP designation if it is not misleading and the firm's full legal name appears in the same materials.
whatToDo: If you brand with a trade name, show your full legal firm name (with LLC or LLP) somewhere in the same website, letterhead or ad.
quote: A law firm may use a trade name which does not specifically include the law firm’s professional entity designation
note: Pre-2020; the only post-2015 Nebraska opinion on advertising/firm names found in the committee list.

body: The Florida Bar, Board of Governors
title: [Permissible payments to for-profit qualifying providers (lawyer referral / matching services)]
text: A lawyer may pay a lead or matching service a fixed fee per period, click or referral, but not a percentage of fees or a flat fee per case accepted.
whatToDo: Pay lead and matching services only fixed fees not tied to whether you are hired or how much the case is worth.
quote: a reasonable, pre-arranged fixed charge for each time a consumer views information about a specific lawyer, commonly referred to as “pay-per-click”
note: Issued by the Board of Governors on inquiries; landmark pre-2020 opinion still listed on the Bar site. Pre-2020 included as the controlling Florida word on lead-generation payments.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Committee on Attorney Advertising
title: Attorney Advertisement Claiming "Expertise" and "Specialization" in an Area of Law (Superseding Opinion 7)
text: Lawyers may say they 'specialize' or have 'expertise' if provable, but only certified lawyers may say 'expert'; Super Lawyers-type listings do not prove expertise.
whatToDo: Use 'specialize' or 'expertise' only if you can document the education and experience behind it; drop 'expert' unless you are certified.
quote: Only lawyers who are certified by the Supreme Court or an organization approved by the American Bar Association may call themselves "experts."
note: Pre-2020 landmark; still the controlling NJ opinion on specialist/expert claims.

body: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Legal Ethics
title: Ethical considerations regarding a lawyer’s participation in an online attorney-client matching service
text: A lawyer may list fixed-fee services on a matching site, but may not let it hold the client's advance fee or pay it a share tied to the legal fee.
whatToDo: Keep client fees in your own trust account and pay matching sites only reasonable advertising costs not based on your fee.
quote: A lawyer must not participate in a program whereby the lawyer pays a for-profit business entity a portion of the legal fee charged to the
note: Pre-2020 landmark on Avvo Legal Services-type matching services; approved by the Supreme Court of Virginia.

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Online Review Solicitation Service
text: A lawyer may use a paid service that asks clients for reviews and posts only positive ones, if clients give informed consent before their contact details are shared.
whatToDo: Get each client’s informed consent before giving a review service their contact details, and explain how the service works.
quote: a lawyer may participate in an online service for soliciting client reviews that collects and posts positive reviews to increase the lawyer’s ranking on internet
note: Pre-2020 landmark on review-solicitation services. Since this opinion, the FTC rule on consumer reviews (16 CFR Part 465, in force October 21, 2024) bans some forms of review suppression, and Google's review policy bars selectively soliciting positive reviews; check both before using a review-gating service.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Lawyer Communication of Juris Doctor Degree, Other Academic Degrees, and Professional Licenses
text: A lawyer may list other earned degrees or licenses in law-practice ads if truthful, but may not use them to imply a legal specialty.
whatToDo: List other degrees or licenses only if true, and never use them to suggest you are a certified specialist.
quote: A lawyer may not use other earned academic degrees or professional licenses to state or imply that the lawyer is a specialist
note: Pre-2020. Withdraws Adv. Op. 94-3.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Lawyer and Firm Website Domain Names
text: A domain name is advertising; it may not imply a specialty the lawyer lacks or name a city where the firm has no active office.
whatToDo: Pick domain names that do not suggest certification or a city where you have no real office.
quote: The registration and publication of a domain name is a form of advertising and a professional designation
note: Pre-2020 landmark; still the Ohio opinion on domain names.

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Direct solicitation by a 501(c)(3) nonprofit law firm offering below-market flat fees]
text: A nonprofit law firm may not directly solicit people who are not its members for paid work, even at low flat fees, because any fee is still pecuniary gain.
whatToDo: Do not make in-person or live calls to strangers for paid work, even if you are a nonprofit charging low fees.
quote: Providing legal services on a reduced fee, below-market, or flat-rate fee basis is no indication that a significant motive for the solicitation is not for
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection.

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Participation in Website Directories and Rating Systems that include Third Party Reviews
text: A lawyer may join online directories and rating systems if the profile information is truthful and not misleading, and the lawyer is responsible for profile content.
whatToDo: Claim and check your directory profiles, and fix anything untrue or misleading.
quote: Opinion explains when a lawyer may participate in an online rating system, and a lawyer’s professional responsibility for the content posted on a profile on
note: Pre-2020 landmark on directories and ratings.

body: Connecticut Bar Association, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Nominal Value Gift for Client Referrals
text: A small after-the-fact thank-you gift, like a logo coffee mug, to someone who referred a client is not payment for a referral.
whatToDo: Keep referral thank-yous to low-cost branded items given after the referral; never offer fee discounts or cash for referrals.
quote: We conclude that giving a gift of such nominal value does not violate the Rules of Professional Conduct.

body: West Virginia Lawyer Disciplinary Board
title: Participation in Attorney-Client Matching Services
text: Paying an online matching service a "marketing fee" that is due only when the legal work is finished is an improper referral and endorsement fee and fee-split with nonlawyers.
whatToDo: Do not join matching sites that take a fee tied to finishing the client’s matter or that hold client fees.
note: Pre-2020 landmark on Avvo Legal Services-type platforms. The official copy on the ODC website is an image-only scan with no text layer, so checkquote.py cannot verify any quote; quote is null. Text was read visually from the page images of the official PDF.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Lawyer-Owned Lawyer-Referral Service
text: A lawyer may own and help manage a for-profit lawyer-referral service with conditions, but the service may not give legal advice to callers while screening them.
whatToDo: If you own a referral service, keep its screeners from giving legal advice and keep it separate from your own practice.
quote: Because a referral service itself is not licensed to practice law, it may not provide legal advice to the public.

body: Los Angeles County Bar Association, Professional Responsibility and Ethics Committee
title: Law Firm Using Former Partner's or Shareholder's Name
text: A law corporation or LLP may keep the name of a lawyer who is no longer an owner but still works at the firm; that is not misleading.
whatToDo: You may keep a former partner's name in the firm name only if that lawyer still works at the firm.
quote: It is not misleading to the public, and therefore is not a violation of the
note: Pre-2020 included as the controlling county-bar opinion on firm names with former partners.

body: San Diego County Bar Association, Legal Ethics Committee
title: [Marketing to mass disaster victims through targeted social media ads]
text: Lawyers may run geographically targeted social-media ads to disaster victims soon after a disaster if the ads are truthful and include required information; California has no waiting-period rule.
whatToDo: If you run geo-targeted ads after a disaster, keep them truthful, label them as ads, and never promise results.
quote: Lawyers may use geographically targeted advertisements to market their legal services on general social media sites so long as the advertisements are truthful

body: Colorado Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: Office Sharing and Virtual Offices
rules: Colo. RPC 7.1(a); Colo. RPC 7.5(a); Colo. RPC 7.5(d)
text: Office-sharing lawyers must not use names, signs or listings that suggest one firm, and virtual-office lawyers must not imply they staff an office they rarely use.
whatToDo: If you share space or use a virtual office, make your name, sign, letterhead and listings show you are separate and say how the office is actually used.
quote: Colo. RPC 7.5(a) extends the prohibition against false and misleading names to letterhead or other professional designations.
note: Source PDF on the bar site carries a '2011' file name but its text shows the 2018 revision.

body: Board of Professional Responsibility of the Supreme Court of Tennessee
title: Legal Services Websites
text: A site where clients post legal jobs and lawyers pay fixed membership and per-quote fees appears to comply if it recommends no lawyer and takes no case-linked fees.
whatToDo: Use bid or marketplace sites only if you pay flat fees, the site does not pick or vouch for you, and your listing is marked as advertising.
quote: appears to comply with the Tennessee Rules of Professional Conduct if it is operated in accordance with the conditions and guidelines set forth in this
note: Issued 2018; Tennessee's only formal opinion on online lawyer-marketplace platforms. Conditions are adopted from an Ohio letter of guidance.

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Letters to employees suggesting they may have claims like the lawyer's clients]
text: A letter or email to non-clients that claims to seek information is a written solicitation if it is really meant to get hired.
whatToDo: Treat 'fact-finding' letters to possible claimants as solicitations and follow the written-solicitation rules for them.
quote: a lawyer's written, electronic or digital communication with a nonclient that purports to seek information may be treated as a written solicitation
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection.

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Firm name including a part-time legislator]
text: A firm may keep a part-time legislator's name if the lawyer practices regularly out of session, but not if the lawyer has mostly stopped practicing.
whatToDo: Keep a lawyer's name in your firm name only while that lawyer still practices regularly with the firm.
quote: When a lawyer is no longer actively and regularly practicing law, including her name in the firm name may be a misleading communication

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Chiropractor paying part of a lawyer’s advertising costs in exchange for client referrals]
text: A chiropractor may help pay for a lawyer’s ads in exchange for referrals, if the lawyer discloses the relationship and gets each affected client’s informed consent in writing.
whatToDo: If another business helps pay for your ads, tell clients about the deal and get their written consent before referring them.
quote: Lawyer may accept financial assistance from the chiropractor to facilitate the dissemination of advertisements on behalf of the Lawyer
note: Pre-2020; included as the controlling South Carolina opinion on non-lawyer co-funding of ads. Page shows no issue date; year taken from the opinion number.

body: San Diego County Bar Association, Legal Ethics Committee
title: [Calling prospective clients referred by a registered lawyer referral service]
text: A lawyer may phone a person referred by a State Bar-registered lawyer referral service, because the person started the contact by asking the service for a lawyer.
whatToDo: It is fine to call people a certified referral service sends you; do not cold-call people who have not asked for help.
quote: Lawyers may directly contact prospective clients they have no previous relationship with when the clients initiate the communication by contacting a registered lawyer referral service

body: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel (Supreme Court of Missouri)
title: lawyer providing educational seminars; solicitation; misconduct through acts of another
text: A lawyer may teach a seminar, but promoting the lawyer's services or handing out discount certificates there is banned in-person solicitation, even if a nonlawyer co-presenter does it.
whatToDo: At seminars you present, have information available on request but do not pitch your services or hand out discounts; follow up only by mail that meets Rule 4-7.3.
quote: The promotion of Attorney’s services or offering of a discount certificate at the seminar would constitute in-person solicitation prohibited by Rule
note: Published informal opinion summary; advisory and not binding per the site. Only the year (2018) is shown. Pre-2020 opinion included because the brief asks for every 2015-2026 Missouri advertising/solicitation opinion.

body: Office of Legal Ethics Counsel (Supreme Court of Missouri)
title: referral fees not permitted; division of fees with another lawyer
text: A Missouri lawyer may not pay a referral fee to the lawyer who sent a case, but may split the fee if Rule 4-1.5(e) is met.
whatToDo: Do not pay pure referral fees; split fees with a referring lawyer only by proportion of work or joint responsibility, with the client's written consent.
quote: Attorney A may not pay a referral fee to Attorney B.
note: Published informal opinion summary; advisory and not binding per the site. Only the year (2018) is shown. Pre-2020 opinion included per the brief (every 2015-2026 Missouri opinion on referrals).

body: The Florida Bar, Board of Governors (on recommendation of the Board Review Committee on Professional Ethics)
title: [Avvo Advisor is a lawyer referral service under Bar rules]
text: The Board decided that Avvo Advisor, which charged a $39 consult and kept a $10 marketing fee, is a lawyer referral service under Florida's rules.
whatToDo: Before joining a platform that sends you clients for a fee, check whether it complies with Florida rules for referral services or qualifying providers.
quote: the Avvo Advisor online system for connecting potential clients with questions to lawyers meets the Bar’s definition of a referral service
note: Board of Governors decision known only from The Florida Bar News report on the Bar site (no separate opinion text found). The year 2017 is inferred from the January 1, 2018 article date; the article does not state the year of the meeting. Pre-2020 landmark on platforms.

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [$99 / Zero Down bankruptcy advertising; post-petition fee contracts]
text: Advertising a '$99' or 'Zero Down' Chapter 7 bankruptcy without more is misleading, because the price leaves out the filing fee and later required work.
whatToDo: If you advertise a low starting price, say clearly what it does not cover, including court fees and later required work.
quote: advertisement of a "$99" bankruptcy or a "Zero Down" bankruptcy is misleading under Rule 7.1 because the price refers only to the filing of the

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Referral service taking a fee-based cut]
text: Under the rules then in force, a service selling fixed-fee legal help and keeping a service-based cut of the lawyer's fee was improper fee-sharing and paid referral.
whatToDo: Do not join a platform that takes a share of your fee unless it is approved under Utah's current rules and Standing Order No. 15.
quote: The service described above violates Rule 5.4's prohibition on splitting fees with a non-lawyer.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Paying nonlawyers for a recommendation or referral
text: A lawyer may not pay the Avvo Legal Services marketing fee as it then stood, because part of that fee pays for a recommendation.
whatToDo: Before joining any platform, check whether its fee pays it to recommend you; if so, do not join.
quote: A lawyer may not pay the current marketing fee to participate in Avvo Legal Services, because the fee includes an improper payment for a recommendation
note: Pre-2020 landmark: widely cited Avvo opinion; relied on in N.Y. State 1267 (2024).

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Lead generation; lawyer paying for-profit company for leads
text: A lawyer may pay a for-profit website for leads if lawyers are picked by clear mechanical methods, the site recommends no lawyer, and the site follows the ad rules.
whatToDo: Use lead services only if they pick lawyers mechanically, never recommend you, and their site follows the ad rules.
quote: A lawyer may pay a for-profit service for leads to potential clients obtained via a website on which potential clients provide contact information
note: Pre-2020 landmark: the NYSBA page states it overrules N.Y. State 902 (2012) as to payment of a marketing fee; followed in N.Y. State 1294 (2026).

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Advertisement with URL and No Other Identifying Information
text: A billboard need not show the lawyer’s name, firm, or office address if its web address leads to a site where that information is easy to find.
whatToDo: If an ad shows only a web address, make sure the landing page clearly names the responsible lawyer and office address.
quote: a billboard advertisement need not contain the lawyer’s name, firm name, or the firm’s office address if the URL address on the advertisement lands on
note: Pre-2020; included as the controlling North Carolina opinion on URL-only ads.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Attorney Newsletters
text: A mainly educational newsletter is not an ad, but a newsletter mainly about the firm’s cases, people or wins is an ad and must follow the ad rules.
whatToDo: Keep newsletters educational, or label and handle them as ads if they mostly promote the firm.
quote: If the primary purpose of a law firm’s newsletter is educational, it does not constitute an advertisement
note: Pre-2020 landmark: controlling NYSBA opinion on newsletters as advertising.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Advisory Committee on Professional Ethics, Committee on Attorney Advertising, and Committee on the Unauthorized Practice of Law (joint)
number: ACPE Joint Opinion 732 / CAA Joint Opinion 44 / UPL Joint Opinion 54
title: Lawyers Participating in Impermissible Lawyer Referral Services and Providing Legal Services for Unregistered Legal Service Plans - Avvo, LegalZoom, Rocket Lawyer, and Similar Companies
text: New Jersey lawyers may not join Avvo's legal-services programs, whose per-matter fee is fee-sharing and a paid referral, or unregistered LegalZoom or Rocket Lawyer plans.
whatToDo: Do not join platforms that take a cut of each legal fee or run unregistered legal service plans; flat advertising fees are the safe model.
quote: New Jersey lawyers may not participate in the Avvo legal service programs because the programs improperly require the lawyer to share a legal fee with

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Text Message Advertising
text: A lawyer may advertise through a text-message service that lets the user start a live phone call, if the texts follow the ad rules and other laws.
whatToDo: Text ads are allowed, but keep them truthful and comply with federal and state texting laws.
quote: lawyers may advertise through a text message service that allows the user to initiate live telephone communication
note: Pre-2020; included as the controlling North Carolina opinion on texting. Rule references reflect numbering before later North Carolina rule amendments.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Solicitation of Professional Employment Via Email
text: A lawyer may solicit clients by email, and may let a referral or advertising service send it, but the lawyer is responsible for its content.
whatToDo: If you or a vendor send solicitation emails, review the content yourself and follow the solicitation rules.
quote: A lawyer may use email to solicit professional employment, subject to the restrictions contained in the Rules of Professional Conduct
note: Pre-2020 landmark. Updates and withdraws Opinion 2004-1.

body: Philadelphia Bar Association, Professional Guidance Committee
title: A lawyer's right to share legal fees with a referring nonprofit organization whose exclusive purpose is to provide legal services
text: A nonprofit whose only purpose is providing legal services counts as a law firm, so lawyers may share fees with it as a referral fee if Rule 1.5 is met.
whatToDo: You may pay a referral share to a nonprofit legal services group that refers cases, but not to for-profit nonlawyer referrers.
quote: a nonprofit organization which provides exclusively legal services is considered a "law firm" within the Rules and, as such, may receive a referral fee
note: Month only on the opinion.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Advertisement of Contingent Fee Arrangements
text: A lawyer may not advertise "no fee unless we win" if the client must repay costs regardless of outcome, unless the ad has a disclaimer explaining that duty.
whatToDo: If clients repay case costs no matter what, do not say "no fee unless we win" without a clear cost-repayment disclaimer.
quote: a disclaimer is required in the advertisement that explains the client’s obligations for repayment
note: Pre-2020 landmark. Withdraws Opinion 98-9.

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Advertising "Best Lawyers", "Super Lawyers" and similar designations and badges]
text: A lawyer may advertise an award like Best Lawyers only if the standards are objective and disclosed, the date and source shown, and nothing was paid for it.
whatToDo: Show awards only with the year, the publisher, and a link to the selection standards, and never pay to get the award.
quote: Yes, the lawyer may accept and advertise such a designation or accolade, and utilize any “badges,” symbols, or other marks authorized by the designating entity
note: Pre-2020; included as the controlling South Carolina opinion on awards and badges. Page shows no issue date; year taken from the opinion number.

body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Former judge's use of judicial title or image in public communications]
text: A former judge in private practice may not use a judicial title or image that implies current judicial status, though a truthful bio may mention past service.
whatToDo: If a lawyer at your firm is a former judge, say "former" or "retired" and avoid robe or bench images that suggest a sitting judge.
quote: a lawyer may not ethically use a judicial title or image implying a current judicial status when the lawyer is not an actively serving judge

body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Internet domain names and website addresses]
text: Domain names and web addresses are public communications about legal services and must not be false or misleading under MRPC 7.1.
whatToDo: Choose domain names that are truthful and not misleading.
quote: Internet domain names and website addresses are a form of public communication concerning legal services that must comply with MRPC 7.1.
note: Pre-2020; the Michigan opinion on domain names.

body: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
title: Social Media I: Marketing and Personal Use
text: Promotional social media must follow the ethics rules; lawyers must fix false content on pages they control, answer reviews without confidences, and endorse others only truthfully.
whatToDo: Review the social media pages you control, remove false endorsements, and never reveal client secrets when answering reviews.
quote: Social media sites, postings or activities that mention, promote or highlight a lawyer or a law firm are subject to and must comply with the
note: Companion Opinion 371 (Social Media II) addresses use of social media in providing legal services, not marketing, and is excluded.

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association, Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility Committee
title: Settlement Agreements Containing Confidentiality or Non-Disparagement Clauses and Their Effect on Lawyer Marketing for and Representing Future Clients
text: Lawyers may not publicize identifying facts of a client's case in marketing without consent, but may advertise the types of matters they handle.
whatToDo: Get client consent before naming a case or its facts in marketing, and describe practice areas rather than unverifiable win counts against named parties.
quote: a non-disparagement clause or confidentiality clause cannot preclude advertisement of areas of practice
note: Month only on the opinion.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Client Testimonials in Lawyer Advertising and Online Services
text: Client testimonials are allowed if not misleading, testimonials stating settlement or verdict amounts are misleading, and a lawyer must remove false or misleading reviews on sites the lawyer controls.
whatToDo: Use testimonials with a disclaimer, never quote dollar results in them, and remove misleading reviews from sites you control.
quote: Client testimonials in an advertisement that state the amount of a settlement or verdict are inherently misleading even if a disclaimer is used
note: Pre-2020 landmark. Withdraws Opinions 89-24 and 2000-6.

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association, Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility Committee
title: Ethical Considerations Relating to Participation in Fixed Fee Limited Scope Legal Services Referral Programs
text: Lawyers may not join Avvo Legal Services-type programs where the company collects the client's fee and takes a marketing fee that rises with it; that is fee-sharing.
whatToDo: Avoid platforms that hold your client's fee or take a percentage-style 'marketing fee'; pay only flat advertising or per-lead costs that do not depend on what you earn.
quote: the amount of the "marketing fee" varies directly with the amount of the flat fee for the legal services.
note: Document served from the PBA's own document host (linked from the pabar.org Ethics Opinions Search page). Month only on the opinion.

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Using the name of a multi-firm organization (verein) as a Texas firm name]
text: A Texas firm may not use a multi-firm network's name that includes people who were never lawyers in the Texas firm; disclaimers do not cure it.
whatToDo: Do not practice or advertise under a network or affiliation name that lists lawyers who were never in your firm.
quote: may not use the name of the organization as their law firm's name on pleadings or other public communications
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection.

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Responding publicly to a former client's negative online review]
text: A lawyer may answer a former client's negative online review only with a short, restrained reply that reveals no confidential information.
whatToDo: When you get a bad review, reply briefly without any client details, or do not reply at all.
quote: The lawyer may post a proportional and restrained response that does not reveal any confidential information
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection.

body: State Bar of Wisconsin, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Advertising and Solicitation in Law-Related Services Owned by Lawyer
text: A lawyer who also runs a financial planning business may mention her law practice in its marketing, but may not offer legal services in person to its clients.
whatToDo: If you own a side business, you may note your law practice in its ads, but do not pitch legal work in person to its customers.
quote: may indicate that the lawyer has a law practice in the marketing materials for the law
note: Pre-2020; the only Wisconsin opinion since 2015 squarely on advertising/solicitation found on the State Bar list.

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [E-mailing members of the Bar to seek client referrals]
text: A firm may e-mail other Rhode Island lawyers asking for referrals; lawyer-to-lawyer e-mails are neither ads nor solicitations, but must still be truthful and follow the specialization rule.
whatToDo: Referral-request e-mails to other lawyers are fine; keep them accurate and avoid improper specialist claims.
quote: Sending e-mails to members of the Rhode Island Bar for the purpose of seeking referrals of clients is permitted under the Rules of Professional Conduct.

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Using a competing lawyer's name as a search-engine advertising keyword]
text: Buying a competing lawyer's or firm's name as a search-ad keyword does not by itself break the Texas rules, but the ad text must not be false or misleading.
whatToDo: You may bid on competitor names as keywords in Texas, but keep the ad text truthful and do not imply you are the competitor.
quote: A lawyer does not violate the Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct by simply using the name of a competing lawyer or law firm as
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection. Expressly disagrees with North Carolina 2010 FEO 14.

body: State Bar of Georgia, Formal Advisory Opinion Board
title: [Sole practitioner firm names using "Group", "Firm" or "& Associates"]
text: A solo lawyer may not use "Group" or "& Associates" in a firm name because they falsely suggest other lawyers, but may use "Firm".
whatToDo: If you practice alone, drop "Group" or "& Associates" from your firm name; "Law Firm" is fine.
quote: The above-referenced Formal Advisory Opinion No. 16-3 was filed by the State Bar of Georgia on June 14, 2016
note: Opinion text read in the State Bar of Georgia online Handbook (https://www.gabar.org/handbook/, Formal Advisory Opinion No. 16-3), which loads its text with scripts, so checkquote cannot see it. The quote is therefore taken from the Supreme Court order PDF hosted on gabar.org. Proposed as FAO No. 15-R1.

body: Ohio Board of Professional Conduct
title: Lawyer Participation in Referral Services
text: A lawyer may not join an online nonlawyer referral service charging a per-service or percentage 'marketing fee' unless it is registered with the Supreme Court of Ohio.
whatToDo: Before joining an online legal marketplace, check its fee model; avoid per-matter or percentage fees unless it is a registered lawyer referral service.
quote: a fee structure that is tied specifically to individual client representations that a lawyer completes or to the percentage of a fee is not permissible
note: Pre-2020 landmark (Avvo Legal Services-type platforms).

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey, Committee on Attorney Advertising
title: Attorney Advertising of Awards, Honors, and Accolades That Compare a Lawyer's Services to Other Lawyers' Services - Reminder From the Committee on Attorney Advertising
text: Comparative awards may be advertised only if the issuer really looked into the lawyer's fitness, with the methodology, issuer name and the Supreme Court disclaimer.
whatToDo: Follow the 2021 reminder, which repeats and expands this notice.
quote: This inquiry into the lawyer's fitness must be more rigorous than a simple tally of the lawyer's years of practice and lack of disciplinary history.
note: Notice to the Bar, not a numbered opinion.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Firm Names—Retired Partner Mediator
text: A firm may keep a retired partner's name in the firm name and list the retired partner as available only as a mediator, if that is not false or misleading.
whatToDo: Keeping a retired partner's name is fine if you state accurately what that person now does.
quote: These rules permit the use of Lawyer A’s name in the firm name as long as the use of the name is not false or

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Offering free bail bond and warrant information to attract visitors to a law office]
text: A lawyer may advertise and give free bail-bond and warrant-check information to office visitors; it is not paying to solicit, but the offer must be honored.
whatToDo: If you advertise free information, give it to everyone who asks, never make it depend on hiring you, and supervise staff who hand it out.
quote: A lawyer does not violate the Texas Disciplinary Rules of Professional Conduct by offering and giving free information about bail bonds and warrants to the
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection.

body: Maryland State Bar Association, Committee on Ethics
title: [Online fixed-fee legal services programs and per-service "marketing" fees]
text: Paying an online fixed-fee legal services company a 'marketing' fee that is charged only when a client hires you and varies with the service is improper fee-sharing with a nonlawyer.
whatToDo: Avoid platforms that charge a per-matter fee that rises with your legal fee; flat advertising fees are allowed.
quote: a fee paid to participate in an online fixed-fee legal services program constitutes fee-sharing if the fee is contingent upon a client retaining a lawyer

body: Maryland State Bar Association, Committee on Ethics
title: Whether a lawyer can pay a fee to an online legal directory for increased visibility throughout the website, including on other lawyers' profile pages?
text: A lawyer may pay an online directory for extra visibility, including ads on other lawyers' profiles, if the ads are truthful and fees are not tied to successful referrals.
whatToDo: Paid directory upgrades are fine if the price is not tied to signed clients; keep your profile accurate.
quote: there is no direct solicitation of business and the paid level advertisement is not tied to successful referrals

body: South Carolina Bar, Ethics Advisory Committee
title: [Fixed-fee referral service run by an attorney directory website; per-service marketing fee]
text: A lawyer may not join a directory's fixed-fee service that collects the client's fee and keeps a per-service marketing fee; that splits fees and pays for referrals.
whatToDo: Do not join platforms that hold your client’s fee or take a cut that varies by the service you perform.
quote: the arrangement would violate the Rule 7.2(c) prohibition of paying for a referral and is not saved by the exceptions
note: Pre-2020 landmark (the Avvo Legal Services-type model); widely cited (e.g., by Florida Op. 18-1 and WV L.E.O. 2018-01). The opinion does not name the platform. Page shows no issue date; year taken from the opinion number.

body: State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct (COPRAC)
title: Attorney Blogging
text: A blog is advertising when it is on the firm website or invites readers to hire the lawyer; a stand-alone blog is not unless it signals availability for hire.
whatToDo: Treat any blog on your firm site, or any blog post that invites readers to hire you or details case results, as an ad that must follow the advertising rules.
quote: unless the blog directly or implicitly expresses the attorney’s availability for professional employment

body: Washington State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Ethical Practices of the Virtual or Hybrid Law Office
text: A virtual lawyer may list an accurate P.O. box or business-center address in ads, but may not imply a firm or local office that does not exist.
whatToDo: Use an accurate address in ads and say if you do not meet clients in person there.
quote: a lawyer working virtually may use a post office box, private mailbox, or a business service center as an office address in advertisements
note: Mostly about virtual practice generally; advertising section is one part.

body: Rhode Island Supreme Court Ethics Advisory Panel
title: [Advertising slogan "Win with [lawyer's name]"]
text: Rhyming slogans like 'Win with [name]' are not false or misleading because a reasonable person would not read them as promising to win every case.
whatToDo: Short upbeat slogans are allowed, but pair them with a results disclaimer and do not promise outcomes.
quote: The Panel does not believe that there exists a substantial likelihood that a reasonable member of the public would conclude from the inquiring attorney's rhyming

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Website email links and warnings to prospective clients about confidentiality]
text: A Texas firm need not post a no-confidentiality warning on website email links, but without an accepted warning it may have to treat what prospects send as confidential.
whatToDo: Put a clear click-to-accept notice before your website contact form or email link if you want to be free to use unsolicited information.
quote: a law firm is not required to include in the law firm's web site a notice warning persons who use the web site's email links
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection.

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Paying an internet service a nominal fee to bid on legal work]
text: A Utah lawyer may pay a small per-bid fee to an online service to bid on legal work, if conflicts are checked and prospects' information is kept confidential.
whatToDo: You may use pay-per-bid sites, but run a conflict check and protect what prospective clients tell you.
quote: Using such an internet business to seek new clients does not violate Rule 1.18 or other rules of professional conduct

body: West Virginia Lawyer Disciplinary Board
title: Social Media and Attorneys
text: Lawyers may advertise on social media but must follow the same rules as elsewhere, must not solicit by real-time electronic contact, and may form prospective-client relationships online.
whatToDo: Treat social media posts and messages like any other ad, avoid real-time solicitation, and use warnings when inviting people to share case details.
note: Pre-2020 landmark (cited by Florida Op. 20-1). Only parts of the 24-page opinion were read (sections on advertising/solicitation, prospective clients, and the conclusion). The official copy on the ODC website is an image-only scan with no text layer, so checkquote.py cannot verify any quote; quote is null. Text was read visually from the page images of the official PDF.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Dual Professions, Yellow Pages Advertising
text: A lawyer-mediator may also advertise under a counselors heading if the ad is not misleading and shows the lawyer's status as a lawyer offering mediation.
whatToDo: When you advertise under a non-legal category, say clearly that you are a lawyer.
quote: must reflect Lawyer’s status as a lawyer offering services as a family mediator.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Insurer-Employed Lawyers' Firm Name
text: Insurance-company staff lawyers may not use a name like 'A & B, Attorneys at Law' without disclosing they are employees of the insurer.
whatToDo: If you are staff counsel, show your employer relationship on letterhead and pleadings.
quote: Courts in other jurisdictions have held that failure to identify lawyer employees of an insurer is misleading.

body: Illinois State Bar Association, Professional Conduct Advisory Opinions
title: Links on a lawyer's website to other businesses or organizations
text: A law firm's website may include links to other businesses or organizations.
whatToDo: You may link to other businesses on your site, but keep the overall site truthful.
quote: A law firm’s website may contain links to other websites of other businesses and/or organizations.
note: Pre-2020; included as Illinois' only opinion on website links.

body: Connecticut Bar Association, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Lawyer's Participation in a Barter-Exchange Program
text: A lawyer may join a barter exchange with uniform membership and transaction fees, but must make sure its listings and solicitations follow the advertising rules.
whatToDo: If you list on a barter or member network, check that its ads about you are accurate, name your licensing states, and that it does not solicit in person for you.
quote: The attorney should monitor the actions and communications relating to attorney services of the Barter Exchange with Members and ensure continued compliance with the advertising

body: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
title: Sharing of Legal Fees With a Lawyer Referral Service
text: A lawyer may pay a referral service a flat fee per referral, but a percentage only to a qualifying nonprofit or as a true lawyer referral service's usual charge.
whatToDo: Pay referral services flat fees; pay a percentage only to a qualifying nonprofit lawyer referral service.
quote: A lawyer may remit a percentage of fees earned on a matter referred to her by the inquiring "lawyer referral service" only if such fees

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Offering Prospective Client a Computer Tablet in Direct Mail Solicitation
text: A lawyer may not offer a free computer tablet to prospective clients in a direct-mail solicitation letter.
whatToDo: Do not offer gifts or prizes to people in solicitation letters.
quote: a lawyer may not offer a computer tablet to a prospective client in a direct mail solicitation letter
note: Pre-2020; included as the controlling North Carolina opinion on inducements in solicitations. Rule numbers as cited in the opinion (pre-2019 numbering).

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Compensating clients to rate lawyer on Internet website
text: A lawyer may give clients a $50 bill credit for rating the lawyer on a site like Avvo if the credit does not depend on what they write.
whatToDo: Any reward for a review must be the same whatever the review says, and clients must write it themselves.
quote: A lawyer may give clients a $50 credit on their legal bills if they rate the lawyer on an Internet website such as Avvo
note: Pre-2020 landmark: see also N.Y. State 1286 (2025) on nominal gifts for Google reviews.

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Attorney Web Sites and Other Electronic Advertising
text: Website content, domain names, web and email addresses, banners and pop-ups are advertising and must follow the Hawaii advertising rules.
whatToDo: Treat your website, domain name and online ads as advertising and check them against HRPC 7.1-7.5.
quote: Communications covered by this Opinion include, but are not limited to: domain names; web addresses; e-mail addresses
note: Hawaii formal opinions are binding on the bar per the Disciplinary Board site.

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Captive Law Firms
text: An insurance-company staff lawyer may not use a firm name, letterhead or business card that suggests an independent law firm.
whatToDo: If you are insurer staff counsel, make your employment status clear on all names and letterhead.
quote: uses a firm name, letterhead, business card, or other professional designations that state or imply that he or she practices in a separate independent law

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Of Counsel
text: Lawyers may use 'of counsel' or similar titles on letterhead, cards and ads only for a continuing, close and regular relationship, and must state any jurisdiction limits.
whatToDo: Use 'of counsel' only for a real ongoing relationship and note licensing limits.
quote: is permissible as long as the relationship between the two is a continuing, close, and regular relationship and the use of the title is not

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Sharing Office Space
text: A lawyer may share office space and staff with nonlawyers if the businesses stay distinct to the public and the nonlawyer does not solicit or feed cases to the lawyer.
whatToDo: If you share space with non-lawyers, keep separate identities and never let them steer clients to you.
quote: so long as the separate business entities are distinct to callers and visitors and the nonlawyer does not solicit for or feed cases to the

body: Disciplinary Board of the Hawai'i Supreme Court
title: Referral Fees
text: A lawyer may not accept a fee from a nonlawyer business for referring a client to it, even with disclosure and consent.
whatToDo: Never take a referral fee from realtors, advisors, medical providers or other vendors you send clients to.
quote: is prohibited from accepting a fee for referring the client to a third-party provider of non-legal services or products.
note: Concerns referral fees the lawyer receives (outbound referrals), not payments for marketing.

body: New York County Lawyers Association, Professional Ethics Committee
title: The ethical implications of attorney profiles on LinkedIn
text: A LinkedIn profile listing only education and jobs is not an ad, but adding practice areas, skills or endorsements likely makes it one; lawyers must remove inaccurate endorsements.
whatToDo: Treat a LinkedIn profile that lists practice areas, skills or endorsements as an ad, and delete endorsements that aren't accurate. New York dropped the set 'Attorney Advertising' label on June 1, 2026.
quote: A LinkedIn profile that contains only one’s education and current and past employment does not constitute Attorney Advertising.
note: Read the full opinion text on nycla.org.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Solicitation
text: Answering an online request for a lawyer, in the way invited, is advertising, not solicitation; posts seeking plaintiffs are allowed except about a specific incident during the waiting period.
whatToDo: Reply to online requests for a lawyer only in the way the person asked, and treat the reply as an ad.
quote: a New York lawyer may respond in the manner invited by the potential client. A response invited by the potential client does not constitute “solicitation,”
note: Pre-2020 landmark: key NYSBA opinion on responding to online requests for a lawyer.

body: Supreme Court of New Jersey (on recommendation of the Committee on Attorney Advertising)
title: Amendments to Attorney Advertising Guideline 2
text: Direct-mail solicitations must print 'ADVERTISEMENT' at the top, larger than the text, and on the envelope, which may carry only basic name and address details.
whatToDo: On solicitation letters, print 'ADVERTISEMENT' two font sizes larger than the body text and keep the envelope to names, addresses and that word.
quote: The envelope shall contain no language other than the lawyer's name, firm, and address; the word "ADVERTISEMENT"; and the recipient's name and address.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Firm Names: Office Sharing with Separate Practices
text: Lawyers who only share office space may not call themselves associates or of counsel to each other or use a joint name like 'A, B & C, Lawyers'.
whatToDo: Do not use a shared firm-style name or letterhead with office mates who are not truly your firm.
quote: is misleading if no law firm exists in which all three lawyers are a part because that is what the name suggests.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Multistate Law Firm, Advertising Availability of Out-of-State Lawyer
text: A multistate firm may advertise its out-of-state lawyers to Oregon clients but may not suggest they are Oregon bar members when they are not.
whatToDo: List each lawyer's licensing states accurately on your website and ads.
quote: A firm may not state or imply, however, that an out-of-state lawyer is, in fact, a member of the Oregon State Bar unless this is

body: Colorado Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: Ethical Responsibilities of Lawyers Who Engage in Other Businesses
rules: Colo. RPC 5.7; Colo. RPC 7.1; Colo. RPC 7.2; Colo. RPC 7.3
text: If a lawyer's side business is not kept clearly separate from the practice, its ads and solicitations must follow the lawyer advertising rules.
whatToDo: Market any side business under its own name, website and ads, with clear disclaimers, or follow the lawyer ad and solicitation rules for it.
quote: the lawyer's communications regarding the law-related service, including advertising and solicitation of customers, must comply with Rules 7.1 through 7.3.

body: Utah State Bar, Ethics Advisory Opinion Committee
title: [Attorney rating systems: 'Best Lawyer' / 'Super Lawyer']
text: A lawyer may advertise a rating only if the rater checked fitness, nothing was paid, the method is public, and the ad says 'included in', not 'the best'.
whatToDo: Say 'named to' a ranking, never 'the best lawyer'; never pay for a rating itself; link to how the rating is chosen.
quote: Any advertisement must state that the lawyer was included in a "super" or other such list or ranking rather than describe the lawyer as being
note: Pre-2015 landmark (issued Nov. 2014): still the controlling Utah opinion on ratings per Op. 22-02.

body: New York State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Responding to a former client’s critical commentary on a website
text: A lawyer may not reveal a former client’s confidential information just to answer that client’s criticism on a lawyer-rating website.
whatToDo: Answer bad reviews without revealing anything confidential about the client.
quote: A lawyer may not disclose confidential client information solely to respond to a former client’s criticism of the lawyer posted on a lawyer-rating website.
note: Pre-2015 landmark: no later NYSBA opinion on responding to negative online reviews was found in the NYSBA listing; cited by D.C. Op. 370 (2016).

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association, Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility Committee
title: Ethical Obligations for Attorneys Using Social Media
text: Lawyers may use social media, accept and answer reviews if they monitor accuracy, and give or ask for endorsements; practice-promoting posts are subject to the ethics rules.
whatToDo: Monitor reviews and endorsements on your profiles, correct inaccurate ones, and treat any practice-related social media post as lawyer advertising.
quote: Attorneys may generally comment or respond to reviews or endorsements , and may solicit such endorsements.
note: Pre-2015 landmark: still the PBA's main formal opinion on social media and reviews. Month only on the opinion.

body: New Hampshire Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: Providing Discounted Legal Services Through "Group Coupon" or "Daily Deal" Services
text: A lawyer may offer discounted services through a group-coupon site's 'coupon deal' if ethical concerns are handled, but a prepaid voucher deal is unlikely to comply.
whatToDo: If you use Groupon-type promotions, sell only a discount coupon (client pays you later), not a prepaid voucher for legal services.
quote: The Committee believes that it is unlikely that a prepaid deal could be structured to comply with the Rules.
note: Pre-2015 landmark: still the NHBA's only opinion on group-coupon marketing.

body: State Bar of Michigan, Standing Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Coupon-type (daily deal) marketing of legal services]
text: Selling legal services through a coupon company that keeps part of the price is improper fee sharing with a nonlawyer.
whatToDo: Do not sell your services through daily-deal coupon sites that take a cut of the fee.
quote: A lawyer's participation in a marketing arrangement in which consumers purchase coupons for legal services from a vendor that retains a portion
note: Pre-2015 landmark (2014) included because it is still the Michigan opinion on coupon/daily-deal marketing; no later Michigan opinion on this found.

body: Bar Association of San Francisco, Legal Ethics Committee
title: [Responding to a negative online review by a former client]
text: A lawyer may respond generally to a former client's online review once the matter is over, without confidential information; if it is still open, a substantive reply may be inappropriate.
whatToDo: Answer negative reviews only in general terms and never share client details.
quote: An attorney is not ethically barred from responding generally to an online review by a former client where the former client's matter has concluded.
note: Pre-2015 landmark (county bar).

body: Pennsylvania Bar Association, Legal Ethics and Professional Responsibility Committee
title: Lawyer's Response to Client's Negative Online Review
text: A lawyer may not reveal client confidential information when answering a negative online review without the client's informed consent; any reply should be short and restrained.
whatToDo: Reply to bad reviews, if at all, with a brief note that confidentiality prevents a point-by-point answer, and never share case details.
quote: a lawyer cannot reveal client confidential information in response to a negative online review without the client's informed consent
note: Pre-2015 landmark: still the PBA's controlling opinion on responding to reviews; cited by the NHBA in 2020.

body: Vermont Bar Association (advisory ethics opinions; committee name not shown on the opinion)
title: [Paid listing in an accident smartphone app that shows nearby injury lawyers]
text: A firm may buy a geographic listing in a car-accident app showing nearby injury lawyers, since the app recommends no lawyer, if later contact follows the solicitation rules.
whatToDo: Paid directory or app listings sold by area are fine if the vendor does not pick or recommend you; keep any follow-up contact within the solicitation rules.
quote: As presented, this arrangement does not trigger the VRPC 7. 2(b)(2) legal service referral considerations.
note: Pre-2015 landmark: the VBA's advertising topic page lists no later advertising opinion, so this remains the latest VT committee word on paid lead/listing apps.

body: Washington State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: Participation in online lead generation services
text: A lawyer may pay an internet lead generator flat, monthly or per-click fees if it does not vouch for the lawyer and matches on disclosed objective criteria.
whatToDo: Use lead services that match on objective criteria and do not vouch for you; avoid ones that pick lawyers for clients.
quote: Lawyer may pay others for generating client leads, such as Internet-based client leads, as long as (1) the lead generator does not recommend, endorse, or
note: Pre-2015 landmark on lead generation.

body: State Bar of Nevada, Standing Committees on Lawyer Advertising
title: Lawyer Advertising Interpretive Guidelines
rules: RPC 7.1; RPC 7.2; RPC 7.3; RPC 7.4; RPC 7.5; RPC 7.2A; RPC 7.2B
text: Past results need a disclaimer and must reflect money the client received; actors and dramatizations must be labeled; only certified specialists may say 'specialist' or 'expert'.
whatToDo: Before running a Nevada ad, check it against these guidelines: label actors and dramatizations, add past-results disclaimers, and do not call yourself a specialist unless certified.
quote: any person appearing or speaking as though he or she were a client of the advertising lawyer or firm must be an actual client
note: Pre-2015 item included as still-controlling guidance: it is the advertising committee's current published interpretive guidance on the bar's Lawyer Advertising page. Not a numbered ethics opinion.

body: Colorado Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: Referral Fees and Networking Organizations
text: A Colorado lawyer may not pay referral fees, but may pay a nonprofit referral service's usual charges and join cooperative marketing that is not a disguised referral service.
whatToDo: Do not pay for referrals; check that any marketing vendor or networking group is advertising, not a disguised paid referral service.
quote: The lawyer also must use reasonable efforts to ensure that companies purporting to provide advertising of the lawyer's services are not in fact improper referral
note: Pre-2015 landmark (revised 2013) still listed without withdrawal on the bar's formal opinion index.

body: Connecticut Bar Association, Professional Ethics Committee
title: Use of a Call Recording Service
text: A lawyer may use a pay-per-call service that records prospective-client calls only if the vendor cannot access the recordings and no third party hears them without consent.
whatToDo: If your call-tracking vendor records intake calls, get a contract term that the vendor cannot access recordings, and limit who can listen.
quote: Pursuant to Rules 1.6 and 1.18, the contract must provide that Yellow Pages will not have access to the recordings
note: Pre-2015 landmark: the only CBA opinion on recording prospective-client calls; no later CBA opinion found on the index.

body: Los Angeles County Bar Association, Professional Responsibility and Ethics Committee
title: Ethical Duties of Lawyers in Connection with Adverse Comments Published by a Former Client
text: A lawyer may reply publicly to a former client's negative online comment only if the reply reveals no confidences, does not harm the client, and stays restrained.
whatToDo: Reply to bad reviews briefly and politely without revealing anything about the client's matter.
quote: the attorney may publicly respond to such comments as long as the rebuttal:  (1) does not disclose any confidential information
note: Pre-2015 landmark (county bar). docDownload link redirects to a signed S3 PDF.

body: North Carolina State Bar (Ethics Committee; adopted by the State Bar Council)
title: Use of Search Engine Company's Keyword Advertisements
text: It is dishonest, and a rules violation, for a lawyer to buy another lawyer’s name as a keyword to trigger the lawyer’s own search ads.
whatToDo: Do not bid on any competing lawyer’s name in search-ad campaigns in North Carolina.
quote: it is a violation of the Rules of Professional Conduct for a lawyer to select another lawyer's name as a keyword
note: Pre-2015 landmark still controlling in North Carolina on competitor keywords.

body: Connecticut Bar Association, Professional Ethics Committee
title: Martindale.com Client Review Ratings
text: A lawyer may send clients to rate him on Martindale.com; client-written reviews are not the lawyer's ad unless the lawyer shapes or answers them.
whatToDo: You may ask clients for reviews on third-party sites, but do not write or edit them, and make sure any response you post is accurate.
quote: Obligations under Rule 7.1 and 7.2 arise only when the lawyer has a hand in creating, shaping or publishing online client reviews.
note: Pre-2015 landmark: the CBA's only opinion on client review sites; no later CBA opinion found on the index.

body: Vermont Bar Association (advisory ethics opinions; committee name not shown on the opinion)
title: [Shared marketing agreement with a realtor and lender]
text: A lawyer may split ad costs with realtors or lenders if payments cover only real marketing costs, the ads imply no partnership, and referrals follow the reciprocal-referral rules.
whatToDo: In co-marketing deals, pay only your fair share of actual ad costs, review the ad content, and never suggest you are in business with the partner.
quote: The advertisements must not state or imply that the lawyer is in business or partnership with the nonlawyer.
note: Pre-2015 landmark: no later VBA opinion on co-marketing found.

body: State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct (COPRAC)
title: Social Networking
text: A lawyer's social media posts are advertising when they offer the lawyer's services, such as posting wins and inviting calls, and the ad rules still apply.
whatToDo: Assume posts that mention wins or invite people to hire you are ads; add any required disclaimers and keep them truthful.
quote: restrictions imposed by the professional responsibility rules and standards governing attorney advertising are not relaxed merely because such compliance might be more difficult or awkward
note: Pre-2015 landmark.

body: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Legal Ethics
title: Is it ethical for a lawyer to become a member of a lead-sharing organization?
text: A lawyer may not join a lead-sharing group, such as a networking club, where membership depends on giving members referrals.
whatToDo: Avoid networking groups that require you to pass a quota of client leads; general professional networking is fine.
quote: membership in such an organization compromises the lawyer’s independence, potentially creates undisclosed conflicts of interest, and violates solicitation rules
note: Pre-2015; included only because it appears still to be the controlling Virginia opinion on lead-sharing groups (no later LEO on point found). Committee opinion, not Court-approved. Rule numbers are those cited in the opinion (pre-2013 Virginia numbering; 7.3(d) was then the paid-recommendation rule).

body: Colorado Bar Association, Ethics Committee
title: The Applicability of Colo. RPC 7.2 to Internet-Based Lawyer Marketing Programs
rules: Colo. RPC 7.1; Colo. RPC 7.2; Colo. RPC 7.2(b); Colo. RPC 7.3(d)
text: A lawyer may pay for an online directory that says it is advertising and charges fixed fees, but not a service that recommends lawyers or charges per client hired.
whatToDo: Before joining an online lead or listing service, confirm it is a neutral, labeled directory with a flat fee, not a paid 'referral' that picks lawyers for clients.
quote: The pivotal point is the distinction between "on-line directory listings" and a for-profit "referral service."
note: Pre-2015 landmark: still listed without withdrawal and cross-referenced by Op. 106 as the Colorado opinion on internet marketing programs.

body: Minnesota Lawyers Professional Responsibility Board
title: Use of the Word “Associates” in a Law Firm Name
text: Using "Associates" in a firm name is misleading unless at least two lawyers practice there, and "& Associates" needs at least three.
whatToDo: Drop "Associates" or "& Associates" from your firm name unless you have enough practicing lawyers to back it up.
quote: the use of the phrase “& Associates” in a firm name, letterhead or other professional designation
note: Adopted before 2015 but amended in 2022 and still the controlling Minnesota opinion on 'Associates' in firm names. The LPRB index lists no other advertising opinions.

body: Alaska Bar Association, Ethics Committee (adopted by Board of Governors)
title: Use of Membership in Lawyer Ranking System In Lawyer/Law Firm Advertising
text: Lawyers may mention Super Lawyers, Best Lawyers or similar rankings in ads only in a set format that gives the publication name, date, and practice area.
whatToDo: Write ranking claims as 'Name was selected for inclusion in [Publication] [Year] in [practice area]'.
quote: so long as the reference includes the publication name, date, and the practice area, if one was specified, in which the lawyer was ranked or
note: Pre-2015 landmark; still Alaska's controlling opinion on ratings in ads.

body: Delaware State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Compensation of a law firm's nonlawyer marketing professional]
text: A firm may not pay its nonlawyer marketing employee bonuses calculated as a percentage of firm revenues or of revenue from clients the marketer brings in.
whatToDo: Pay marketing staff and vendors salary or flat fees, not a percentage of the fees they bring in.
quote: Compensation of a Law Firm's marketing professional may not be based upon a percentage formula based on total revenues received from new or old clients
note: Pre-2015 landmark included because the DSBA issued no later opinion on marketing compensation (no opinions 2012-2020 per the index). Quote is from the committee's summary page at the front of the PDF.

body: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Legal Ethics
title: Obligations of a Lawyer Who Receives Confidential Information Via Law Firm Website or Telephone Voicemail
text: Listing an email or phone does not invite secrets, but a website form asking for case details can create duties, so firms should use a clear click-through disclaimer.
whatToDo: If your website intake form asks for case facts, make visitors click to accept a plain disclaimer saying no lawyer-client relationship or confidentiality is created before they submit.
quote: including an e-mail address on a law firm’s website or publishing a telephone number in a yellow-page advertisement, without more, is not the solicitation of
note: Pre-2015 landmark: the VSB still cites it on its ethics page (https://vsb.org/Site/lawyers/ethics.aspx) for communications with website visitors. It predates any Virginia Rule 1.18 on prospective clients; whether a later rule change affects it was not checked.

body: Delaware State Bar Association, Committee on Professional Ethics
title: [Advertising "Super Lawyer" and "Best Lawyer" designations]
text: A lawyer may advertise being named a 'Super Lawyer' or 'Best Lawyer' if the ad states the year and practice area of the designation and otherwise follows the advertising rules.
whatToDo: When you show a Super Lawyers or Best Lawyers badge, state the year and the practice area it covers.
quote: as long as the lawyer states the year and particular specialty or area of practice of the designation
note: Pre-2015 landmark included because it is the only DSBA opinion on lawyer ratings and no later one exists.

body: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
title: Participation in Internet-Based Lawyer Referral Services Requiring Payment of Fees
text: Lawyers may join online referral services charging flat participation, per-name or per-client fees, if the fee is not a share of legal fees and listings are not misleading.
whatToDo: Pay online referral or lead services only flat fees, never a share of your legal fee, and check what they say about you.
quote: Lawyers may participate in both not-for-profit and for-profit lawyer Internet-based referral services where the services require a flat fee for participation
note: Pre-2015 landmark: still the controlling D.C. opinion on paid online referral services; relied on in D.C. Op. 369 (2015). Inquiry Nos. 06-01-24 and 06-08-11.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Internet Advertising: Payment of Referral Fees
text: The Oregon State Bar withdrew this internet-advertising referral-fee opinion in 2018; its text is no longer published.
whatToDo: Do not rely on this opinion; check current RPC 7.2 and later opinions instead.
quote: Internet Advertising: Payment of Referral Fees [WITHDRAWN 2018]
note: Only the withdrawal notice is posted; the original holding could not be read, so no holding is stated.

body: State Bar of Texas, Professional Ethics Committee
title: [Paying to join an internet service that forwards potential clients' information to paying lawyers]
text: A Texas lawyer may pay an online service that forwards potential clients' problems to paying lawyers only if it meets the opinion's conditions, which the lawyer keeps checking.
whatToDo: Before buying leads from an online service, confirm it does not pick lawyers for clients, charges a reasonable advertising fee, does not cap participants, and label your first contact as advertising.
quote: a lawyer may pay a fee to participate in an internet client-lawyer connection service of the type described in this opinion
note: Read on the Texas Center for Legal Ethics site, which hosts the Committee's full official opinion collection. Pre-2015 landmark included because it is still the Texas Committee's main opinion on paid online lead services and the State Bar's Advertising Review page still links it.

body: District of Columbia Bar, Legal Ethics Committee
title: Firm Names for Solo Practitioners
text: A solo lawyer may use any trade name that is not false or misleading, and using the word "firm" is not misleading by itself.
whatToDo: Choose a firm name that does not mislead clients about the size or nature of your practice.
quote: The use of the word "firm" in the firm name does not inherently constitute a misleading representation about a solo practitioner.
note: Pre-2015 landmark: D.C. opinion on trade/firm names for solo practitioners; no later D.C. opinion on this topic found in the 210-present index. Inquiry No. 05-03-01.

body: Virginia State Bar, Standing Committee on Lawyer Advertising and Solicitation (former); approved by the Supreme Court of Virginia
title: Communications to the Public Involving a Lawyer's Recognition by a Listing in a Publication such as The Best Lawyers in America
text: A lawyer may advertise a truthful Best Lawyers-type listing, but may not claim to be 'the best', credit the whole firm, or tout a credential anyone can buy.
whatToDo: Name the exact listing and year, describe it in plain words, and do not turn one lawyer's listing into a firm-wide 'best' claim.
quote: Lawyers may advertise the fact that they are listed in a publication such as The Best Lawyers in America.
note: Pre-2015 landmark included because the VSB says it is the only Legal Advertising Opinion still in force (status confirmed on https://vsb.org/Site/lawyers/ethics.aspx). The Rule 7.1 text quoted in the opinion is the pre-2013 version; later Virginia rule changes were not checked against it.

body: State Bar of California, Standing Committee on Professional Responsibility and Conduct (COPRAC)
title: Implied Formation Through Communications Sent via Website
text: A lawyer inviting website questions owes confidentiality unless a plain-language disclaimer defeats visitors' reasonable belief; a bare 'no attorney-client relationship' click-through is not enough.
whatToDo: Put a clear, plain-English warning on web intake forms that what visitors send will not be kept confidential (if that is your policy), not just 'no attorney-client relationship.'
quote: may effectively disclaim owing a duty of confidentiality to web-site visitors only if the disclaimer is in sufficiently plain terms
note: Pre-2015 landmark on website intake disclaimers.

body: Oregon State Bar, Board of Governors (Legal Ethics Committee)
title: Information about Legal Services: Initiating Contact with Lawyer-Referral Service Clients
text: The Oregon State Bar withdrew this opinion on lawyers contacting referral-service clients in 2018; its text is no longer published.
whatToDo: Do not rely on this opinion; check current RPC 7.3 instead.
quote: Information about Legal Services: Initiating Contact with Lawyer-Referral Service Clients [WITHDRAWN 2018]
note: Only the withdrawal notice is posted; the original holding could not be read.

body: Oklahoma Bar Association, Legal Ethics Committee
title: [Listing jury verdict and settlement amounts in advertising]
text: Ads may state verdict or settlement amounts if accurate and not confidential, with an equally prominent disclaimer that each case is different.
whatToDo: Before advertising a verdict or settlement, make sure it does not reveal client confidences, check the figure, and add an equally prominent 'each case is different' disclaimer.
quote: An attorney may list in an advertisement, specific amounts awarded by jury verdict if the following requirements are met
note: Pre-2015 landmark: no later OBA formal opinion on advertising found (okbar.org/ethics/ethics-opinion-no-331 through -338 return 404; the 2014 topical index lists nothing later on advertising). The opinion quotes pre-2008 Rule 7.1 text; Oklahoma's current Rule 7.1 wording was not checked against it. Pre-2015 landmark. Its Rule 7.1 quotation predates later amendments; current Oklahoma Rule 7.1 was not checked against it.

body: Kentucky Attorneys' Advertising Commission
title: False, Deceptive and Misleading Advertising
text: The Commission's regulation lists ad content it may treat as misleading, including actors posing as clients, misleading area codes, and verdict amounts without the case facts.
whatToDo: In Kentucky ads, do not show verdict amounts without the case facts, do not let actors look like real clients, and disclose where your office really is.
quote: Statements that may create unjustified expectations include advertisements concerning results obtained on behalf of a client, such as the amount of damage award
note: A Commission regulation (guideline), not an ethics opinion. No adoption or amendment date is shown on the document, so it may predate 2015; included because it is the Commission's current published advertising guidance.

body: Kentucky Attorneys' Advertising Commission
title: Advertising of Fees
text: A 'no fee unless we win' ad must say the client may owe costs, and a stated contingent-fee percentage must say whether it is before or after costs.
whatToDo: Next to any 'no fee unless you win' line, add that clients may owe costs and expenses, and say how the percentage is calculated.
quote: the advertiser must include language stating the client may be responsible for court costs and/or case expenses
note: A Commission regulation (guideline), not an ethics opinion. No adoption or amendment date is shown on the document.
